items.title: Laws & policy surface — design + data-model stub (v0.1.2 expanded-prototype groundwork)
items.summary: Roadmap v0.1.2 expanded-prototype groundwork (Ben, 2026-07-09 refocus). First pass at the law / policy surface: what a law IS as a data object and how it gates or modifies economic (and later political) behaviour. Design-forward + data-model stub only — no committed mechanics — so the v0.2.0 nation actor and the v0.3.0 political layer land on prepared ground. Design-owed: the law-object schema, the prototype lever set, and the enforcement seam are all open. SETTLED 2026-08-02: laws are enacted by NATIONS and the player (a corporation) is a law SUBJECT until BL-094 — which contradicts BL-171 confirmed intent that Tax is a player lever, so Tax becomes a read-only display of the home nation regime while Wages stays a real lever (a private contract term, not a law, sitting above law #8 floor). NR-024. Effect is a closed TAGGED UNION over the four families (closed because the taxonomy was derived from instances and the price-clamp veto depends on it staying closed). Prototype cut: all ten representable, exactly TWO enacted (extraction tax, labour-contract floor) because the other eight need UI that does not exist. Margin modifiers accumulate as a SUMMED rate applied once, never successive multiplications, or order-independence fails. Difficulty 3->4.
items.design:
**Theme (roadmap v0.1.2).** Define the **law / policy** surface as a first-class data object: a law is a named, serialisable record that gates or modifies behaviour (initially economic — tax, tariff, subsidy, extraction cap — later political). This item settles the *shape*, not the mechanics.

**Scope.** Design + a data-model stub only. Enumerate the law-object schema (id, subject, condition, effect), sketch a small prototype lever set, and name the enforcement seam in the economy step where a law would read. No UI, no active law effects committed — the point is to position the model.

**Open questions.** Law-object schema; which levers are prototype-worthy vs deferred; where enforcement hooks into `economy_system` without breaking determinism; how laws relate to the future filter system (BL-087) and the nation actor (BL-094) that will own them.

**Standing-rule note.** Policy proper is post-prototype scope (TECH_FOUNDATIONS); this is the design + stub that precedes it, not the system. **Authority:** docs/SYSTEMS.md once landed.

### Shared condition-set + tangible law list (2026-07-11, mobile session, Ben)

**Object shape.** A law = **`condition_set`** (the shared predicate — see BL-156 for the full triple; here it is the enactment / applicability gate) **+ a polymorphic `effect`**. The condition side is settled by BL-156; the design genuinely new to Laws is the **effect taxonomy** and the **enforcement seam**. Both fall out of a concrete law list rather than being invented abstractly.

**Ten tangible laws (price clamps 5–6 vetoed 2026-07-11, Ben).** Grouped by effect family — the list *is* the effect taxonomy, derived from instances:

*(a) Margin modifiers — scale a flow's price/cost*
1. **Extraction tax** — per-unit levy on raw extraction output. Effect: −margin on extraction.
2. **Production subsidy** — per-unit credit on a target resource's processing. Effect: +margin / −effective input cost.
3. **Import tariff** — duty on goods arriving by convoy from off-body. Effect: +cost on inter-body imports.
4. **Export duty** — levy on goods shipped off-body. Effect: +cost on exports (retains supply locally).

*(b) Quantity clamps — bound a flow or stock*
5. **Extraction cap** — ceiling on extraction rate from a body / deposit (conservation). Effect: clamp yield.
6. **Strategic reserve mandate** — withhold N units of a resource from market before sale/export. Effect: reserve floor on stockpile.

*(c) Cost adders — per-building / per-tick overhead*
7. **Emissions levy** — cost scaling with industry density on a body (ties to the habitability feedback). Effect: +upkeep on polluting buildings.
8. **Labour-contract floor** — minimum workforce cost (minimum wage). Effect: +per-building labour cost.

*(d) Gates — binary allow/deny*
9. **Trade embargo** — ban trade of a resource, or with a named body / nation. Effect: block convoy routes for that good.
10. **Zoning restriction** — cap a building type's count per body, or ban it on a terrain class. Effect: placement-validation gate.

> Price clamps (ceiling / floor) were proposed as family (b) and **cut 2026-07-11** — the effect taxonomy now spans four families, not five. A resolved-price clamp would also be the one effect that fights the supply/demand price resolution directly rather than shifting a flow's cost; the veto keeps every law a *modifier over* the market, never an *override of* it.

Most laws are unconditional once enacted (empty `condition_set` = always-on); the interesting ones gate on world state — a **wartime tax** `(era == war)`, an **emissions levy** that only bites past an industry-density threshold `(structure-density ≥ N)`, a **reserve mandate** triggered by a market-scarcity signal `(market ≤ X)`.

**Determinism seam (the load-bearing call).** Laws are the *first* condition-set consumer a live tick reads (techs are read-only, post-prototype — BL-087 res. 6). Rules: evaluate all active laws' condition-sets at **one fixed point** in `run_economy_step`, producing a resolved modifier set *before* the step consumes it; laws touching one quantity combine **order-independently** (additive rates / defined precedence, never iteration order); `market` / `surplus` subjects read the **previous** tick's resolved values, not mid-tick mutating ones.

**Politics ≈ laws — the v0.1.2 ↔ v0.1.5 boundary (raised 2026-07-10, Ben).** A nation's political character (BL-054, `NATION_GENERATION.md`) can be expressed as a **named preset — a bundle of default law-values** — rather than a separate mechanic: a protectionist nation ships high tariffs + export duties; a statist one, price ceilings + a reserve mandate; a laissez-faire one, near-zero extraction tax + no emissions levy. This dissolves most of the BL-155 ↔ BL-158 overlap. The clean line:

- **Laws (v0.1.2)** own the **mechanism** — the modifier objects and their enforcement seam.
- **Politics (v0.1.5, BL-158)** owns two things: **(a)** named **law-bundle presets** that express character — a Laws *consumer*, not a new object; and **(b)** the inter-nation **relationship / sentiment** axis, which is genuinely *not* a law (a diplomacy state).

So the *economic-behaviour* half of a political profile is laws; only the *relationship* half is new in v0.1.5. BL-158 inherits this framing (its own field to be updated when that minor is reached — authority time-slice).

**Player levers surfaced in the Budget ledger (BL-171, 2026-07-11).** The Budget-ledger redesign ([[BL-171]]) added **Tax** and **Wages** tier selectors to the player Budget view as *stubbed* controls — drawn and selectable, no economic effect — pending this item's mechanics. Confirmed intent (Ben): **Tax** = a **player-set policy lever** (the player picks a tax tier as a deliberate trade-off); **Wages** = a **cost↔workforce trade-off** (a higher wage tier raises the wage cost but improves the workforce — availability / output / retention — moving wages from today's fixed `base_wage` constant to a player lever). These are the first two concrete laws/policies this surface must model; wire them into the ledger controls (ui_state.budget_tax_tier / budget_wage_tier, UI-only today) when this lands.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the effect object, the prototype cut, and WHO ENACTS A LAW


### Sequencing note — this was deliberately deferred, and is being settled anyway

Sprint 2 (2026-07-31) records Ben's call to sequence BL-210's nation rewrite *first*, because
designing policy/military/politics against nations that BL-218 is about to stop being Voronoi
blobs risks rework. That reasoning still holds and is not overturned here.

Settled now on Ben's 2026-08-02 instruction to work through the design-owed set regardless of
deferral, in preparation for a batch delivery. **The rework exposure is real but bounded**, and
bounding it is a design constraint rather than a footnote: everything below is specified against
*nation identity and nation-owned state*, never against how a nation's territory or character was
DERIVED. BL-218 changes the derivation (simulated settlement history in place of Voronoi + a
random politics draw); it does not change that a nation has an id, territory, a character and
relationships. Any part of these designs that would break under BL-218 is a part that reached
into generation, and none of them do.

### The hole nobody has named: a corporation cannot legislate

Working through the prototype lever set surfaced a contradiction between two settled things,
and it has to be resolved before anything is wired.

BL-171 added **Tax** and **Wages** tier selectors to the player's Budget ledger as stubbed
controls, and this item records the confirmed intent that "**Tax** = a player-set policy lever
(the player picks a tax tier as a deliberate trade-off)". But the player is a **corporation**,
and every law in the ten-law list is an instrument of public authority — a tax, a tariff, a
cap, an embargo, a zoning rule. A corporation does not enact those. It is *subject* to them.

**Settled: laws are enacted by NATIONS. The player is a law SUBJECT, not a law author, for the
whole prototype.** BL-094 (v0.2.0) pivots the player to a nation and is the point at which
enacting becomes available; until then the player *reads* the law set and plans around it. That
is also the more interesting prototype — a market shaped by rules you did not choose is a
constraint to route around, which is the Trade dimension doing its job.

This splits the two Budget-ledger controls, which turn out not to be the same kind of object at
all:

- **Wages — a real player lever, and NOT a law.** A corporation genuinely sets what it pays.
  It is a private contract term, so it needs no legislative authority and can ship in the
  prototype exactly as the ledger already draws it. It interacts with law #8 (labour-contract
  floor) as a *floor* the corporation must clear, which is the correct relationship and a good
  demonstration of the whole model: the nation sets the floor, the player chooses where above it
  to sit.
- **Tax — NOT a player lever.** The control as drawn promises something the player cannot have.
  Options, in preference order: (a) re-present it as a **read-only display** of the tax regime
  the player's home nation currently imposes, which makes the ledger honest and the law system
  visible from day one; (b) remove it until BL-094; (c) keep it as a lever and accept that the
  player is legislating for themselves, which is incoherent. **Recommend (a)** — it costs
  roughly what (b) costs, and it turns a broken control into the first surface where laws are
  legible.

Recorded as a decision-taken (NR-024) because it contradicts a previously confirmed intent, and
because it changes a control that is already on screen.

### The effect object: a TAGGED UNION over the four families, not a hierarchy

The ten laws were derived from instances and the four families fall out of them, so the
taxonomy is **closed** — which is exactly the condition under which a tagged union beats a
virtual-dispatch hierarchy. Each family has a uniform parameter shape:

- **(a) Margin modifier** — `(flow_selector, rate)`. Scales a flow's price or cost.
- **(b) Quantity clamp** — `(quantity_selector, bound, is_ceiling)`. Bounds a flow or stock.
- **(c) Cost adder** — `(building_selector, per_tick_amount)`. Per-building overhead.
- **(d) Gate** — `(subject_selector, allow)`. Binary allow/deny.

A closed union serialises trivially (a tag plus a fixed payload — no polymorphic dispatch
across the save seam, which flat binary serialisation would otherwise make painful), is
exhaustively switchable so a new family cannot be added without the compiler naming every site,
and keeps every effect a plain value. That last property is what makes the order-independence
rule below checkable rather than hoped-for.

**A fifth family must not be added casually.** Price clamps were proposed and vetoed
2026-07-11 precisely because they would fight price resolution rather than shift a flow's cost.
The union's closedness is the mechanical expression of that veto.

### The prototype cut: TWO enacted, TEN representable

**All ten laws are expressible in the schema; exactly two are enacted in the prototype.**

- **Labour-contract floor (#8)** — because Wages is already a real player-facing control and
  the floor is what gives it meaning.
- **Extraction tax (#1)** — the simplest margin modifier, on the flow the economy is built
  around, and the one that makes the read-only Tax display show something real.

Everything else is schema-and-serialisation only: representable, round-trippable, inert. The
reason is not caution, it is that **eight of the ten need UI that does not exist** (an embargo
needs a diplomacy surface, zoning needs a placement-rules surface, a reserve mandate needs a
stockpile policy surface). A law nobody can see or react to is not a system, it is a hidden
modifier — and a hidden modifier in an economy the player is trying to read is worse than
nothing.

### Enforcement seam — unchanged, and now with the failure it prevents named

The determinism rules already recorded stand as written: evaluate every active law's
condition-set at **one fixed point** in `run_economy_step`, producing a resolved modifier set
*before* the step consumes it; combine order-independently; `market`/`surplus` subjects read the
**previous** tick's resolved values.

Worth stating what the middle rule is protecting against, because it is the one that will be
violated by accident: two laws touching the same quantity must produce the same result in either
order. Additive rates do; sequential multiplication does not (a 10% tax then a 10% subsidy is
not a 10% subsidy then a 10% tax). **So margin modifiers accumulate as a summed rate applied
once, never as successive multiplications.** That is a one-line rule with a real bug behind it.

### Relation to BL-087 and BL-094

- **BL-087 (filter system, v0.3.0)** inherits the condition-set wholesale (BL-156 settles it)
  and adds the availability-window effect. Nothing here forecloses it.
- **BL-094 (nation actor, v0.2.0)** is where enacting arrives. The law record therefore carries
  an **enacting nation id from the start**, even though nothing writes it but generation — a
  law with no author is not migratable later without touching every saved law.

items.title: Tech system — early design toward the quest/gate model (v0.1.3 expanded-prototype groundwork)
items.summary: Roadmap v0.1.3 expanded-prototype groundwork (Ben, 2026-07-09 refocus). Early design toward the tech / quest system — the condition-set gate model (gate = quest = tech, one object) that BL-087 reframed and that the v0.3.0 filter system will formalise. Design only at this stage: settle the tech-object and gate-condition shape so later work has a spine. Precursor to BL-087 (filter system, v0.3.0). SETTLED 2026-08-02: a CAPSTONE is not a separate object or a bool — it is a tech whose EFFECT opens another tree, so the distinction lives on the axis that is already polymorphic and cannot drift out of sync. Unlocks thread into availability as SET MEMBERSHIP tested at placement validation and recipe selection (a lookup, not a tree walk; monotonic in the prototype; unlocked content is ABSENT rather than disabled-and-visible). BL-087 boundary tabulated: this item settles the OBJECT, BL-087 settles the SYSTEM — no tech UI, no authored trees beyond one worked example, no Era rename here.
items.design:
**Theme (roadmap v0.1.3).** The early-design pass for the **tech system**, feeding the unified gate model BL-087 settled: a **gate = quest = tech** is one condition-set object, so a tech can gate on economic OR world state. This item does the groundwork design; BL-087 formalises it as the filter system in v0.3.0.

**Scope.** Design only — no implementation. Settle the tech / gate-condition object shape, the capstone-vs-ordinary distinction, and how a tech unlock threads into content availability (buildings, recipes, quest trees). Position it so v0.3.0's Era→Filter rename inherits a coherent model.

**Open questions.** Tech-object schema and its overlap with the law object (BL-155); which conditions are expressible in the prototype; how quest trees hang off capstones; the boundary between this precursor and BL-087's full design.

**Relates:** BL-087 (filter system, v0.3.0 — this is its early-design precursor), BL-155 (shared condition-set shape). **Authority:** docs/SYSTEMS.md once landed.

### Shared condition-set — the tech/law predicate unified (2026-07-11, mobile session, Ben)

The 2026-07-08 tech mock (`world/tech_tree.{hpp,cpp}`) stores `condition` as a **single label** (`research | structure | stockpile | market | surplus | era`) — descriptive, not evaluable. BL-155 (Laws) forces the promotion: a law is read every tick and must resolve true/false, so the label must become a **structured predicate**. Settled shape, shared by tech / quest / law / (v0.3.0) filter:

- **`condition_set` = a flat AND-list of atomic conditions** — no nested OR-mesh (mirrors BL-087 resolution 1: binary tree, no re-converging mesh). Keeps evaluation order deterministic and the predicate legible.
- **atomic condition = `(subject, comparator, threshold, sustained_ticks)`**:
  - `subject` — the 2026-07-08 vocabulary reused verbatim: `research` (tech id complete) · `structure` (building exists / count) · `stockpile` (resource ≥ N) · `market` (price / volume signal) · `surplus` (sustained net-positive flow) · `era` (world clock ≥ Era N) · `line-depth` (standing-line tier ≥ N).
  - `comparator` — `≥ / ≤ / == / exists`.
  - `threshold` — number, resource id, tech id, or era ordinal.
  - `sustained_ticks` — default 0 (instantaneous); >0 = must hold N ticks. The Propellant Loop capstone's "sustained surplus" is `(surplus, ≥, X, N)`.

The `condition` **label** already on `tech_node` becomes the `subject` axis of this triple — the vocabulary was the hard part and it is done; this only makes it evaluable. **Effect stays polymorphic** (see BL-155): tech → discrete unlock, quest → opens next tree, law → continuous modifier, filter → availability window. One condition type, many effect types. Direct precursor to BL-087's filter system, which inherits this predicate wholesale.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — capstones, unlock threading, and the BL-087 boundary


### Sequencing note — this was deliberately deferred, and is being settled anyway

Sprint 2 (2026-07-31) records Ben's call to sequence BL-210's nation rewrite *first*, because
designing policy/military/politics against nations that BL-218 is about to stop being Voronoi
blobs risks rework. That reasoning still holds and is not overturned here.

Settled now on Ben's 2026-08-02 instruction to work through the design-owed set regardless of
deferral, in preparation for a batch delivery. **The rework exposure is real but bounded**, and
bounding it is a design constraint rather than a footnote: everything below is specified against
*nation identity and nation-owned state*, never against how a nation's territory or character was
DERIVED. BL-218 changes the derivation (simulated settlement history in place of Voronoi + a
random politics draw); it does not change that a nation has an id, territory, a character and
relationships. Any part of these designs that would break under BL-218 is a part that reached
into generation, and none of them do.

The condition-set — the hard half — was settled 2026-07-11 and is untouched. Three questions
remained.

### Capstone is not a different OBJECT; it is a tech whose EFFECT opens a tree

The tempting move is a `bool is_capstone` or a separate record. Both are wrong for the same
reason: they encode in the schema something that is already visible in the data.

**A capstone is a tech whose effect opens another tree. An ordinary tech's effect unlocks
content.** One object, one effect field, and "capstone" becomes a *description* of a tech's
role rather than a property to keep in sync. A tech that both unlocks a building and opens a
tree is then automatically expressible, and needs no third category.

This also matches the item's own framing that effect stays polymorphic while condition is
shared — the capstone distinction lives on the axis that is already polymorphic, so it costs
nothing.

### Unlock threads into availability as SET MEMBERSHIP, tested at the point of use

A tech's effect names a content id (a building type, a recipe). The unlocked set is the
accumulated union of every completed tech's unlocks, and availability is a membership test at
the two places content is chosen: **placement validation** (the existing placement-rules seam)
and **recipe selection**.

Three properties make this the right shape:

1. **It is a lookup, not a search.** No walking the tech tree at the point of use.
2. **It is monotonic in the prototype** — techs complete and never un-complete, so the set only
   grows and there is no revocation path to get wrong. (BL-087's availability *windows* break
   monotonicity by design; see the boundary below. That is a v0.3.0 problem and the set-based
   shape survives it — a window is a predicate over the same set, not a different structure.)
3. **It serialises as a set of ids**, which round-trips through flat binary without ordering
   hazards provided the walk is sorted.

Content not in the set is **absent, not disabled-and-visible** — consistent with how BL-229 has
just settled rival-building pages (absent rather than blanked): a UI full of things you cannot
use teaches less than a UI that grows.

### The boundary with BL-087, stated so the precursor does not eat the successor

**BL-156 settles the OBJECT. BL-087 settles the SYSTEM.** Concretely:

| This item (v0.1.3) | BL-087 (v0.3.0) |
|---|---|
| Tech record shape, effect taxonomy, capstone-as-effect | The filter system proper, Era to Filter rename |
| The unlocked-set mechanism and its two test points | Availability **windows** (content that closes as well as opens) |
| Serialisation of techs and the unlocked set | Quest trees as authored content, the tree editor/UI |
| One worked example tree, to prove the shape | The full Era 1 content graph (BL-087 own scope) |

**Not in scope here, explicitly:** any tech UI, any authored tree beyond a single worked
example, and the Era rename. The item's own warning about the precursor/successor boundary is
the thing most likely to be violated, because a tech object with no tree to sit in feels
incomplete — it is supposed to.

## EFFECT TAXONOMY AUTHORED 2026-08-05 (docs/research/TECH_EFFECTS.md)

Ben's ask ('these trees should unlock, upgrade, retire, upgrade reconnaissance, open law/tax/automation capacity, begin space, and unlock war and communication doctrines') is the effect taxonomy this item already names as its own scope. Worked out in the research doc; the structural call is that an effect is a PAIR - `(kind, target)` - because the seven categories as stated mix effect KINDS (unlock/upgrade/retire) with subject DOMAINS (reconnaissance, space) and with SYSTEMS that are themselves unlocked (laws, doctrines). Split, they compose; collapsed, they cannot.

**Eleven kinds, closed** (the BL-155 tagged-union precedent, and closed for the same reason - the consumer must switch exhaustively): `unlock` `upgrade` `retire` `modifier` `access` `reach` `intel` `institution` `doctrine` `resource` `open`. `open` IS the settled capstone rule, unchanged: a tech whose effect opens a tree. Seven categories the list omitted, each already implied by an existing doc: placement access (placement_rules), continuous modifiers (the biggest class by count - BL-155's summed-rate machinery), logistics reach (SUPPLY.md), resource realisation (RESOURCES.md's Era split), demography (BL-273), finance and credit terms (FINANCE.md/BL-073), and instrument access (LENSES.md).

**Retirement is the one that fights the settled model** - this item settled a MONOTONIC unlocked set, and retirement breaks it deliberately. Sanctioned mechanism is BL-087's availability windows (a predicate over the same set, not a different structure). Three questions carried to NR-066: grandfathering already-built content, availability-vs-economics (a route nobody builds has retired itself), and reversibility under blockade. Lean recorded: grandfather, retire by window not erasure, and use explicit retirement mostly on units and doctrine branches where exclusion is the point.

What remains is one thing: ASYMMETRIC per-pair sentiment[from][to], asymmetric because BL-225 (seizure costs the seizing nation standing with observers) is inherently directional and a symmetric scalar cannot express "A resents B, B is indifferent". items.design:
**Theme (roadmap v0.1.5).** The thinnest useful **political stub**: the data slots the v0.2.0 nation actor needs to own — political character, inter-nation relationships, and placeholder lever slots — as serialisable records, with no working system behind them yet. The real political layer is promoted in v0.3.0 (politics + the filter system).

**Scope.** Data-model stub only. No political mechanics, no AI decision-making, no diplomacy beyond the existing data-model stub (TECH_FOUNDATIONS). This closes the v0.1.x groundwork band: after it, the model is positioned for the v0.2.0 refocus.

**Open questions.** Political-state schema; overlap with the existing nation generation (BL-054 territory + political-character assignment); which relationship data is worth stubbing now vs at v0.3.0; the boundary between this stub and the v0.3.0 working layer.

**Relates:** BL-094 (the nation actor that owns this, v0.2.0), v0.3.0 politics (the working system this stubs toward), BL-054 (existing nation political character). **Authority:** docs/SYSTEMS.md once landed.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — most of this item was already dissolved; what is left is the relationship axis


### Sequencing note — this was deliberately deferred, and is being settled anyway

Sprint 2 (2026-07-31) records Ben's call to sequence BL-210's nation rewrite *first*, because
designing policy/military/politics against nations that BL-218 is about to stop being Voronoi
blobs risks rework. That reasoning still holds and is not overturned here.

Settled now on Ben's 2026-08-02 instruction to work through the design-owed set regardless of
deferral, in preparation for a batch delivery. **The rework exposure is real but bounded**, and
bounding it is a design constraint rather than a footnote: everything below is specified against
*nation identity and nation-owned state*, never against how a nation's territory or character was
DERIVED. BL-218 changes the derivation (simulated settlement history in place of Voronoi + a
random politics draw); it does not change that a nation has an id, territory, a character and
relationships. Any part of these designs that would break under BL-218 is a part that reached
into generation, and none of them do.

### BL-155 already removed the larger half

The politics-is-laws framing settled 2026-07-11 (BL-155 § Politics ~ laws) means a nation's
**political character is a named law-bundle preset** — a Laws *consumer*, not a new object. A
protectionist nation is high tariffs plus export duties; a laissez-faire one is near-zero
extraction tax and no emissions levy.

So the economic-behaviour half of a political profile needs **no schema of its own**: it is a
preset id plus the law records it expands to. This item inherits that (its own field now updated,
per the authority time-slice rule) and what remains is genuinely one thing.

### The relationship axis: ASYMMETRIC per-pair sentiment

The one piece of political state that is not a law, because a diplomacy state is not a modifier
over a flow.

**Asymmetric — `sentiment[from][to]`, not a symmetric pair value.** Symmetric is half the
storage and is the wrong model, for a reason that already exists in the backlog: **BL-225**
(asset seizure costs the seizing nation sentiment and credit access) is inherently
*directional*. A nation that seizes assets loses standing **with the observers**, and each
observer's reaction differs by how exposed it was. A symmetric scalar cannot express "A resents
B, B is indifferent", which is the ordinary case in the averted-rupture premise (BL-223) the
history ladder produces.

The stub is therefore:

- **`sentiment`** — a fixed-point scalar per ordered pair, one bounded range, no sub-axes.
  (Trust/fear/respect decomposition is a v0.3.0 question; one axis proves the storage.)
- **`character_preset`** — a preset id per nation, expanding to law records via BL-155.
- **No lever slots.** The original scope names "placeholder lever slots"; those are laws, and
  BL-155 owns them. A placeholder for a thing that already has a home is a future
  reconciliation problem.

### Determinism

An N-by-N table over nations, and the default seed now generates **43** of them (up from 14 at
v0.0.3, since BL-221 landed). That is ~1,850 ordered pairs — trivial for storage, but it makes
the walk rule load-bearing rather than pedantic: **any iteration over pairs is a sorted walk
over nation ids**, never over an unordered container, and any aggregate (a nation's average
standing) accumulates in fixed point in that fixed order. This is the same rule as BL-222's
first-industrialiser argmax, and at 43 nations it is the kind of thing that produces a
seed-dependent divergence nobody can reproduce.

### Sizing

Difficulty stays 2. Half the item dissolved into BL-155 and what remains is one table and one
preset id — but it is now correctly the *last* of the four stubs, since it consumes BL-155's
law records and cannot be specified before them.

items.title: Relocate sell-order management from the Building ledger to the market surface
items.summary: Filed 2026-07-09 as the required companion to BL-143 (Building-ledger redesign), which removes the 'Sell Orders' tab from the construction/Building ledger. Sell orders currently live ONLY in draw_sell_orders_section (construction_panel.cpp:361), so removing that tab is a functional regression unless relocated. items.title: Automatic exchange policy — per-resource auto-buy/sell bands (blacklist-default) + relocate sell orders to the market surface
items.summary: Filed 2026-07-09 (Ben, market-exchanges design session; all forks settled by Q&A). The player governor over the already-automatic order book: standing per-(corp,body,resource) inventory-band policies that shape what the auto path does with the player's own stock, blacklist-default, surfaced as a new Market Ledger 'Policy' view. Retires the construction-panel Sell Orders tab into it (BL-143 companion). Axis A of automatic exchanges; Axis B (counterparty) is fast-follow BL-161. v0.2, after the prototype cut.
items.design:
**Settled 2026-07-09 (Ben, market-exchanges design session; five forks resolved via Q&A).** The order book already auto-derives BOTH sides each tick (clear_markets: pool surplus above production auto-sells; processor input shortfalls auto-buy). This item adds the PLAYER GOVERNOR on top — standing policies that bound what the automatic path may do with the player's own stock — and retires the manual sell-order tab into it.

**Axis A — per (player-corp, body, resource) inventory-band policy (the FULL band, Ben's call):** `sell_enabled` + `reserve` (hold >= this; auto-sell only the surplus above reserve + next-run production need) + `floor_price`; `buy_enabled` + `target` (auto-buy UP TO this stock level — speculative stockpiling for a construction draw / a planned convoy, MAY exceed production need) + `ceiling_price`. Between reserve and target: hold. Today's manual sell order is the degenerate one-tick case (enabled, reserve 0, floor).

**Default polarity — BLACKLIST-DEFAULT (Ben's call).** Unconfigured resources auto-trade exactly as today; every player action is subtractive/bounding (blacklist = sell_enabled false -> hold; band = set reserve/target/limits). No dead market on ship day — the current substrate IS the default.

**Mechanism.** A new `derive_exchange_orders(w, policies)` runs each econ tick BEFORE clear_markets, reading policy + current pool + production need and emitting the `player_orders`/`player_buy_orders` overlay that clear_markets ALREADY accepts — no order-book core change. Fully deterministic (world/* standing rule).

**Hard constraint — local-body only, never auto-launches.** SUPPLY.md: space launches are ALWAYS player-directed. Auto-buy-to-target may be satisfied only from the SAME body's market; a policy can never trigger an inter-body convoy. Cross-body acquisition stays a manual convoy decision. (Same-body terrestrial auto-dispatch already exists in the substrate, so this is consistent, not new.)

**Serialisation seam.** Policies are player-authored world state -> a new serialised policy table (flat binary, no SQLite). This makes the item Full-mode, determinism- + save-format-touching; needs a verifier-headless check on derive_exchange_orders and a save round-trip.

**Surface — new Market Ledger 'Policy' view (Ben's call)** beside Prices/Markets/Trends: one inline-editable row per resource (Resource | Sell | Reserve | Floor | Buy | Target | Ceiling) for the selected body's player pool. This is BL-143's 'relocate sell orders to the market surface' home, so REMOVING the construction panel's Sell Orders tab (draw_sell_orders_section) is a REQUIRED companion here — couples to BL-143 (which independently wants that tab gone).

**Scope / sequence.** v0.2 — Ben pushed the whole automatic-exchange feature PAST the prototype cut; v0.1.0 stays audit-only and playtest ships on the current auto-derived substrate without the policy layer. Axis B (counterparty allow/deny — the embargo/Trade->Conflict lever) is the cross-linked fast-follow BL-161.

**Authority** -> docs/SYSTEMS.md § Trade (mechanic) + docs/ui/ledgers/market.md (surface) on landing.

**AI-primitive confirmation (2026-07-26, AI design session).** The inventory-band policy table is also the AI's trade surface: AI corps author the same per-(corp, body, resource) policies via the corp_command seam (AI_OPPONENT.md §5-6) - there is no AI-only trade path. derive_exchange_orders must therefore read policies for ALL corps, not just the player (same mechanism, same determinism; the player UI is just one author of many).

**Buy-order wiring decision (2026-07-31, doc sweep).** The buy half of the BL-037 order book is engine-complete but dormant — app::step_economy passes only ui_state.sell_orders, so no live caller ever submits buy orders (MARKETS.md § Known limitations). Decision: no interim manual buy-order surface. This item's buy band (buy_enabled / target / ceiling_price) IS the player buy surface, and derive_exchange_orders becomes the first live emitter of the player_buy_orders overlay — a manual buy tab built now would be exactly the kind of surface this item retires on the sell side. One call deferred to landing: nothing in this design sets preferred_seller, so the soft 1.10x preferred-seller tolerance stays dormant even after this ships — decide then whether the policy row carries a preferred-seller field, or BL-161's hard allow/deny supersedes the soft hint (retiring the tolerance path).

items.title: Counterparty allow/deny — embargo & exclusive-trade lever (automatic exchanges, Axis B)
items.summary: Filed 2026-07-09 (Ben, market-exchanges design session). Axis B of automatic exchanges — the counterparty control, and the half that turns Trade into a Conflict lever. Per-(player-corp) allow/deny list of rival corps, applied as a match filter; deny-list = embargo, allow-list = exclusive trade. fast-follow to BL-160; realises the counterparty-preference open Brief in SYSTEMS.md § Trade. v0.2.
items.design:
**Settled 2026-07-09 (Ben, market-exchanges design session).** Axis B of automatic exchanges — the counterparty control, and the half that makes Trade a Conflict lever. Fast-follow to BL-160 (Axis A resource bands); realises the 'counterparty preference' open Brief in SYSTEMS.md § Trade.

**Model.** A per (player-corp) allow/deny list of rival corps, applied as a filter inside clear_markets' matching loop (skip disallowed (buyer, seller) pairs). Two modes: DENY-LIST (the common case — refuse to match a named rival: an embargo) and ALLOW-LIST (the extreme — trade ONLY with named corps: an exclusive supply relationship). Complements the existing soft `preferred_seller` +10% tie-hint with a HARD include/exclude.

**Surface.** The action lives on the RIVAL's Selection panel ('Embargo / Trade-only') — where the player is already looking at that competitor (BL-093 made Selection action-first). The BL-160 Policy view reflects the resulting state.

**Serialisation.** The counterparty list is player-authored world state -> serialised alongside the BL-160 policy table (flat binary).

**Scope / sequence.** v0.2, after BL-160 — requires its derive/overlay plumbing.

**Authority** -> docs/SYSTEMS.md § Trade on landing.

**AI-primitive confirmation (2026-07-26, AI design session).** The allow/deny list is per-corp, not player-only: AI corps embargo via the same corp_command verb (AI_OPPONENT.md §5), making embargoes a symmetric Trade->Conflict lever. An AI-initiated embargo should surface in the BL-205 chat log (public channel) - diplomacy as legible messaging, not hidden state.

items.title: Road tier ladder (Track/Road/Highway) + spanning/symmetric road render
items.summary: Filed + built 2026-07-11 (Ben). Two coupled road fixes on the same render/economy path. (1) VISUAL SPAN FIX — the road render ([[BL-147]] ROAD_RENDER_PLACEMENT) drew a centre-to-centre segment only when BOTH a tile and its right/down cardinal neighbour carried a road, over a rectangular offset subset of the true hex adjacency; so diagonal roads read patchy and a segment 'belonged' to a pair, not a tile ('a road from ≠ a road to'). Rewritten so each roaded tile draws its OWN half-edge (centre → shared-hex-edge midpoint) toward every roaded, revealed, land hex-neighbour (all 6): two roaded tiles meet exactly at the edge midpoint = one continuous span, identical whichever tile is 'from'. Render-only — road_level stays a per-tile field (no save-format change). (2) TIER LADDER — the two generated tiers (local/trunk) become a named 3-tier ladder Track(1)/Road(2)/Highway(3), each a distinct cost-discount (road_traversal_multiplier 0.67/0.50/0.40) AND a distinct on-canvas weight/brightness; generation assigns by centre scale, the player places any tier from the build front door (upgrade-in-place allowed). Railroad is a separate transport MODE, not a road tier → [[BL-173]].

items.title: Railroad — a distinct land transport mode (rail lattice + rolling stock)
items.summary: Filed 2026-07-11 (Ben, road-fix thread). Railroad as a transport MODE distinct from the road tiers ([[BL-172]] made Track/Road/Highway cost-discounts on the shared land mode). Rail is not just a cheaper road: it wants its own network (tracks are placed, not a per-tile discount over open land), its own cost/speed profile, and plausibly its own gate (a rail depot at each end, like Port gates Sea). Design-owed. SETTLED 2026-08-02 (all five): rail is a REAL convoy mode, not a fourth road tier — it needs endpoint gating and a hard network, and a tier would have to special-case both. Gated on a rail depot at BOTH endpoints, mirroring the Port gate. A separate rail_level tile field with pathing that traverses ONLY rail between depots — a hard network, not a discount, which is what makes a rail route a strategic object a rival must route around. Nations DO ship with an inter-city backbone: an earth-like 1960 world with no railways is the same lying-world objection BL-263 applied to markets with no cause, and a backbone makes the interesting decision a spur rather than a blank-sheet build. Cross-tie hatching, read as a network at planetary zoom. Difficulty set to 4.
items.design:
**Idea — design owed.** [[BL-172]] settled that Track/Road/Highway are three tiers of the *land* mode (cost-discounts on the A* traversal of otherwise-open land). Railroad is qualitatively different and was deliberately deferred there: a rail line is its OWN network — you travel along laid track, not cheaply across open ground — with a distinct cost/speed profile (very low per-unit cost, high fixed build, bulk-favouring). Open questions to resolve at design: (1) Is rail a new `convoy.mode` value (SUPPLY.md's {land,sea,air,space} → +rail) with its own `base_logistics_cost`, or a fourth road tier with a connectivity constraint? Leaning: a real mode, because rail needs endpoint gating and can't reuse the 'cheaper open-land' model. (2) Gate — a **rail depot / station** building at both endpoints (mirrors Sea's Port gate, SUPPLY.md Infrastructure gates), Era 0. (3) Network model — a separate rail_level tile field + a placement affordance, pathing that can ONLY traverse rail tiles between depots (a hard network, not a discount). (4) Generation — do nations ship with an inter-city rail backbone, or is rail wholly player-built? (5) Render — a distinct glyph (cross-tie hatching) vs the road spans; ICONS/PLANETARY. Mechanically justified via Trade (bulk-freight arbitrage the road tiers can't make marginal). Deterministic (standing rule). **post-v0.1.0** — beyond the prototype's remaining arc; revisit once the road tiers + supply loop are proven in play. Authority → SUPPLY.md when designed. Ben road-fix thread 2026-07-11.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — all five questions

**1. A real mode.** `convoy.mode` gains `rail` alongside {land, sea, air, space}, with its own
`base_logistics_cost`. The item's own leaning is right and the reason is decisive: rail needs
**endpoint gating** and a **hard network**, and the road-tier model is "cheaper traversal of
otherwise-open land". A fourth road tier would have to special-case both, at which point it is a
mode wearing a tier's name.

**2. Gate — a rail depot at BOTH endpoints**, mirroring Sea's Port gate (SUPPLY.md
§ Infrastructure gates). Era 0. Both, not one: a line with one station is not a line.

**3. Network — a hard one.** A separate `rail_level` tile field plus a placement affordance;
pathing between depots traverses **only** rail tiles. Not a discount on open ground. This is the
property that makes rail a strategic object — a rail route is a thing you *built* and a rival
can route around or compete with, rather than a cheaper way to cross terrain everyone shares.

**4. Generation — nations DO ship with an inter-city rail backbone.**

The alternative (wholly player-built) was tempting and is wrong. GENERATION_STRATEGY.md's
economic premise is a **saturated, earth-like base** the Nation AI owns; an earth-like 1960 world
with no railways would be conspicuously, visibly false — the same lying-world objection BL-263
applied to markets with no cause.

It is also the better game. A pre-existing backbone gives the player something to **connect
to**, which makes the interesting decision a spur ("is it worth reaching the trunk?") rather
than a blank-sheet network build. Player-built-only would mean the first rail on the planet is
the player's, which misdescribes the world the premise establishes.

**5. Render — cross-tie hatching**, distinct from the road spans, per ICONS.md's recipe. The
glyph must read as a *network* at planetary zoom, so continuity along a line matters more than
per-tile detail — the same lesson BL-175 slice 1 records about arrows that read as a field.

**Difficulty set to 4** (was unset): a new mode, a tile field, a hard-network pathing case, a
generation pass, and a render. Sequence after BL-172's road tiers are proven in play, as the
item states.

items.title: Planetary Supply lens legibility — flow, not a uniform arrow field
items.summary: Filed 2026-07-11 from the BL-098 walkthrough (US-009, scored 2.5/5 — jointly lowest). The solar-level inter-body route renders as a clean line, but the planetary Supply lens draws an identical '>' arrow on every hex (including ocean) — it reads as noise, not flow. LENSES.md already gates the true render on Layer-5 supply-route rendering. Design-owed. SETTLED 2026-08-02 as TWO SLICES. Slice 1 (no dependency, promotable now): delete the uniform arrow field and render honest-empty with one line — the current render is worse than empty because a glyph on every tile including ocean asserts three false things (supply flows everywhere, uniformly, in one direction). Slice 2 (gated on BL-088): arrows ONLY on traversed tiles with direction taken from the route record, volume by opacity/width not by arrow count, matching the solar rung cyan line one rung down; the US-009 landed-cost friction goes on route hover/selection, not painted on tiles. requires BL-088 records slice 2 only — the item is not blocked.
items.design:
**Friction (BL-098 walkthrough, US-009).** At the *solar* rung the inter-body route is a legible cyan line (Kepler→Pallas); at the *planetary* rung the Supply lens paints a uniform '>' arrow on every tile, ocean included — a field of identical glyphs that communicates no source, sink, or direction. It is actively misleading rather than merely empty.

**Direction (Ben's call — suppress-now vs wait-for-Layer-5):**
- **Near-term (small):** stop drawing the uniform-arrow field until real routes exist, so the lens is honest-empty rather than noise.
- **Full (gated):** directional flow bound to actual persistent trade routes ([[BL-088]]) + per-unit *landed cost* visible at decision time (the US-009 friction), when the Layer-5 supply-route render lands. The solar route line ([[BL-039]]/[[BL-038]] substrate) is the legible half to build from.

**Evidence:** screenshots/supply_lens_planetary_glyphs (noise) vs supply_lens_solar_route (legible line). **post-v0.1.0** because the full fix is Layer-5-gated; the near-term suppression could be pulled earlier if Ben wants. Traces US-009; parent review [[BL-098]]. Authority → LENSES.md.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — two slices, and the honest-empty state is the one that ships first

Ben's framing already gave the shape (suppress now vs wait for Layer 5). Settling it as **two
slices inside this item** rather than leaving one item permanently half-blocked, because the
near-term half has no dependency and fixes something actively wrong.

### Slice 1 (promotable now, no dependency) — stop lying

Remove the uniform `>` field. The lens renders **nothing** on tiles, and shows a single honest
line where the legend sits: *"No supply routes on this body."*

The argument is not that an empty lens is nice; it is that the current one is **worse than
empty**. A glyph on every tile including ocean asserts that supply flows everywhere, uniformly,
in one direction — three false claims. A player who trusts it reasons from noise. Honest-empty
teaches the correct thing (there are no routes yet) in one line.

This also makes the lens's eventual arrival legible: the first real route is a visible change
from nothing, rather than a slight variation in a field that was always there.

### Slice 2 (gated on BL-088 persistent trade routes) — flow, not a field

When routes exist, the render is bound to them and to nothing else:

- **Arrows only on tiles a route actually traverses.** Not a field. The absence of an arrow is
  information.
- **Direction from source to sink**, taken from the route record — the property the current
  render fabricates.
- **Volume by opacity or width, not by count.** One arrow per traversed tile, varying in
  weight; N arrows for N units is unreadable at planetary zoom.
- **The solar rung is the model to match.** BL-039/BL-038's cyan Kepler-to-Pallas line already
  reads correctly, and the planetary render should look like the same system one rung down —
  same colour language, same source/sink logic.

**The US-009 friction (per-unit landed cost at decision time) belongs to slice 2**, on the
route's own hover/selection content rather than painted on tiles. A cost is a number, and
numbers do not belong in a tile overlay.

### Sizing

Difficulty 3 covers both slices; slice 1 alone is a 1. `requires` records BL-088 because slice 2
cannot start without it — but slice 1 is explicitly promotable ahead of that, and the item
should not be read as blocked.

items.title: Corporate borders - HQ-projected influence range and the tall/wide specialisation axis
items.summary: Ben's steer (2026-07-18): corporations should have BORDERS like nations do - a corporate sphere projected outward from HQ building(s) with a RANGE, generalising the player-only home-ring/HQ-star chrome (BL-085) into a real ranged border for every corp on the Corporation lens. A corp opens with ONE HQ and builds more as it advances (tech/laws), which creates a TALL (deepen fewer HQs) vs WIDE (spread more HQs) specialisation axis. A gameplay mechanic - HQ range gates/modifies where the corp can operate - not just a visual layer. Deferred with corporation-system behaviour (post-v0.1.0); captured so the data model + lens rendering position for it.
items.design:
**Why (Ben's steer, 2026-07-18):** nations have real territory (Country lens: tile ownership + borders) but corporations only get tile *tints* on the tiles they directly hold, plus the player-only home-ring/HQ-star chrome (BL-085). Corporations should have **borders too** - a corporate sphere projected outward from **HQ building(s)** with a **range**, symmetric with how nations hold territory.

**Core model.** Every corporation has at least one **HQ** building. Each HQ projects an **influence range** (a radius / cost-field over the tile grid); the **union of a corp's HQ ranges is its border** (its operating sphere). A corp opens with **one HQ**; as it advances it can **build additional HQs**, each extending reach.

**The tall/wide axis (the point).** This is the specialisation lever: **tall** = invest in fewer HQs, deepening range/potency in place; **wide** = build more HQs, spreading the footprint across more territory (and eventually more bodies). Neither is strictly better - the choice shapes the corp's strategic character. This is what the mechanic is *for*.

**A gameplay mechanic, not just a visual.** The border is load-bearing: HQ range **gates or modifies where the corp can operate** (build / extract / project logistics), so it competes spatially with rival corporations and overlays - does not replace - nation jurisdiction. The exact effect is open (see below).

**Extensible via laws + technology.** HQ **range**, the **max HQ count**, and HQ **potency** are all levers laws and tech can move - this is the framework the later Policy/Research systems build on to differentiate corporations. The advancement that unlocks the 2nd+ HQ is itself a tech/law gate.

**Relationship to existing work.** The player-only home-cluster ring + `icons::hq` star (BL-085; CANVASES/PLANETARY) is the *seed* of this - a per-body 'my region' chrome around the player's holdings. This item **generalises** it into a real, ranged border for **every** corporation, surfaced on the **Corporation** lens (LENSES.md - today the lens only tile-tints held tiles + draws a player border) with the `hq` glyph (ICONS.md) marking each HQ.

**Open questions (why this is design-owed, not designed):**
- **Range shape** - fixed radius, or a decaying cost-field like the nation Voronoi-BFS budget (NATION_GENERATION.md)? A cost-field composes better with terrain and reads as 'reach'.
- **What the border gates** - build-only? an extraction/logistics bonus inside it? a hard operate-boundary? This sets how much it constrains vs. flavours play.
- **Overlap rules** - corp spheres vs. nation territory (a corp operating in a foreign nation), and corp-vs-corp overlap (contested tiles).
- **Per-body vs. global** - one HQ per body projecting locally (matches BL-085's per-body chrome), or a home HQ + weaker branch offices elsewhere.
- **Discovery interaction** - the border read against competitor-visibility + the activity fog (DISCOVERY.md: rival buildings visible, internals private).
- **Advancement curve** - which tech/law unlocks each further HQ, and the cost of going wide vs. tall.

**Prototype scope.** Deferred (post-v0.1.0). Corporation behaviour is deferred from the prototype (io-standing-rules.md; nation behaviour parked BL-054), so this lands with the corporation-system work, not before. Captured now so the data model and the Corporation-lens rendering can position for it.

**Files (on landing):** src/world/corporation_generation.cpp (HQ designation + range), the placement/economy seam (operate-gate), src/ui/body_surface_canvas.cpp + ui_state overlay (border render, generalising the BL-085 chrome); docs CORPORATION_GENERATION.md / LENSES.md / GLOSSARY.md / ICONS.md on landing.

**Design resolved (Ben, 2026-07-23) - core settled; the six opens above are answered, two sub-threads stay deferred:**

1. **Range shape -> decaying cost-field.** Potency tapers with distance from HQ. Within the sphere it is a soft gradient; at the ~20% floor construction becomes *impossible* - a hard build-boundary at the edge over a soft potency gradient inside. Composes with terrain, reads as 'reach' (not a fixed radius).

2. **What the border gates -> industry build-validity.** A building is only placeable inside the corp's border. Open sub-question Ben flagged: rather than a hard *extraction* cut-off at the edge, let extraction *taper*. The land-grab risk this raises is NOT solved by the taper but by the origin gate (#3).

3. **Origin gate (new - the anti-land-grab mechanic).** Corporations begin as **national** companies, confined to their home nation's territory. **International** operation is reserved for **1-2 great powers**, tech-gated. This steers the early game away from a 'who clicks the good tile first' free-for-all and gives the tall/wide axis room to grow into. Connects to CORPORATION_GENERATION.md's franchising / nation-seeded-privatisation / Era-sovereignty open items.

4. **Overlap -> tiles belong to both.** No exclusive ownership: a tile can carry a corp border AND nation territory at once. The active lens decides what is drawn - corp border in the corp's identity colour (Corporation lens), nation border in the national colour (Country lens). Because each tile holds only one building, there is **no competition for owned tiles**, so no contested-tile arbitration is needed.

5. **Per-body / structure -> single home HQ + weaker branch offices.** The exact potency of branches vs. the home HQ is a **calibration** left until multiplayer playtest begins.

6. **Discovery -> border implies vision.** Fog and border are mutually exclusive: a corp's border is itself a **vision source**, so it is impossible to have fog inside your own border.

**Deferred sub-threads (captured, not designed):**
- **Tech/law advancement curve** - which unlock gates each further HQ and the international-reach gate, plus the range / potency / max-HQ-count levers. Deferred with the Policy/Research systems.
- **Distance-based logistics bonus** - a proximity advantage (e.g. a steel mill sited near a feeding tile gets a logistics edge). Requires a **tile-to-tile nearness map** - infrastructure worth building regardless; this is one consumer of it. Parked until that map exists.

items.title: Corporate reach layer (visual slice of BL-182) - rival HQ border rings on the Corporation lens
items.summary: The in-scope, render-only first slice of BL-182: under the Corporation lens, each RIVAL corporation on the active body draws an HQ-projected border - a reach ring centred on its HQ (the holding nearest its holdings centroid) plus an hq star, in the corp's identity colour, radius = holdings extent + a fixed projected range. Extends the always-on player-only home ring/HQ star (BL-085) to rivals so corporations read as having borders too. The player's own border stays the BL-085 home ring (excluded here to avoid a double-draw). Gates nothing, mutates no state - the gameplay mechanic stays deferred in BL-182.

items.title: Road-tier legend — teach the Track/Road/Highway read on the Planetary canvas
items.summary: Filed 2026-07-19 (design session, Ben) from the deferral explicitly noted at the BL-172 road-tier landing (DEVLOG 2026-07-11): the always-on road layer encodes Track/Road/Highway by thickness + brightness only (SUPPLY.md's three-tier ladder), with no legend or key anywhere in the UI, so the distinction is illegible to a new player. Settled 2026-07-19: contextual read on the tile Selection panel / hover tooltip, not a persistent chip.
items.design:
**Problem.** `body_surface_canvas.cpp`'s always-on road-edge pass renders three tiers (Track/Road/Highway = `road_level` 1/2/3) purely by line weight and brightness (thin+dim to thick+bright, per SUPPLY.md's ladder). There is no legend anywhere naming which is which, and roads are the only always-on canvas layer with a visual code and no key.

**Why it isn't a trivial drop-in.** Roads are deliberately NOT lens-gated - they render always-on like terrain (Ben's call at BL-147 landing), which is exactly why they were left out of the per-lens legend drawer (BL-164's fold-out legend is keyed to `overlay_mode`, so it only shows when a lens is active). Giving roads a legend means picking a home that doesn't imply 'roads are a lens.'

**Options considered:**
1. **Persistent chip** near the minimap/lens strip, always visible regardless of active lens - three swatches + tier name. Simplest to discover, but adds permanent chrome to an already dense corner (the same crowding concern that deferred this at BL-147/172 landing).
2. **Contextual read** in the Selection panel / hover tooltip when a road tile is hovered or selected - zero permanent chrome cost.
3. **One-time teach** - a dismissible callout the first time the player places or reveals a road, then never again. Teaches once, costs nothing after.

**Determinism/save.** Pure UI/render - no save-format or world-state change.

**Authority.** PLANETARY.md's road-render section already documents the tier ladder's visual encoding; this item adds the legend/teaching mechanism there once landed.

### Settled 2026-07-19 (Ben)
**Option 2 - contextual.** When a road tile is hovered or selected, name the tier ("Highway" etc.) and its traversal discount in the existing per-tile read surface - `draw_tile_selection` (`selection_panel.cpp`, the BL-162-adjacent tile mockup work) for the click path, and the existing hover tooltip in `body_surface_canvas.cpp` for the hover path. No new persistent chrome, no new file. Options 1 and 3 dropped.

items.title: Road ↔ commercial-reach fog interaction — should roads dim with tile vision?
items.summary: Filed 2026-07-19 (design session, Ben) from the deferral explicitly noted at the BL-147 road-render landing (DEVLOG 2026-07-10): roads draw full-bright on any survey-revealed tile, including ones the intra-body commercial-reach fog (BL-151/152) would otherwise dim under its analytic wash. Settled 2026-07-19: dim roads by tile vision, same as the lens fill.
items.design:
**Current behaviour.** The Planetary canvas's intra-body reach fog (DISCOVERY.md) derives a per-tile `vision` scalar each frame (1 in the permanent layers - own buildings, the corp-centre-to-market corridor - else the moving convoy beam's intensity); the fog wash applies `(1 - vision)` **over the lens fill**, so a fogged tile's analytic read dims with it. The road-edge pass in `body_surface_canvas.cpp` draws independently of that wash, so a road on a `vision ≈ 0` tile still renders at full brightness - identical treatment to a road on a tile the player actively operates.

**Is this actually wrong?** DISCOVERY.md is explicit that 'Survey owns the unrevealed tiles' and the reach fog's semantics are deliberately 'commercial reach, not unknown terrain' (Ben's call at BL-151 landing) - the home planet is the player's own soil, fog means *where your logistics operate*, not *where the land is unmapped*. A road is arguably physical infrastructure like the tile hex itself (visible once surveyed, never re-hidden), not activity knowledge - in which case full-bright-once-surveyed is correct and the DEVLOG deferral was a false alarm.

**The other reading.** The reach fog's whole point is to make the player's own commercial footprint pop (BL-154: 'your trade spine is always lit'). A road you've never trafficked competes visually with the corridors you actively use; dimming untouched roads the same as the lens fill would sharpen that contrast rather than contradict the fog's intent.

**Options considered:**
1. **Leave as-is** - roads are physical terrain, not activity; close this out by adding a line to DISCOVERY.md/PLANETARY.md stating the exclusion is deliberate, so the deferral doesn't resurface as a phantom bug.
2. **Dim roads by `(1 - vision)`** the same alpha multiply the lens fill already receives, reusing the per-tile `vision` value `body_surface_canvas.cpp` already computes - one multiply in the road draw pass, no new state.

**Determinism/save.** `vision` is already frame-derived, non-serialised VIEW state per DISCOVERY.md's stated invariant (never fed back into `world/*`) - either option is a pure render change.

### Settled 2026-07-19 (Ben)
**Option 2 - dim by vision.** Apply the same `(1 - vision)` alpha multiply the lens fill already receives to the road segment's draw colour in the road-edge pass (`body_surface_canvas.cpp`), reusing the existing per-tile `vision` value - no new state. DISCOVERY.md gains a line noting roads participate in the reach-fog wash like the lens fill, closing the physical-vs-activity ambiguity in favour of 'your own footprint outranks infrastructure you don't use.'

items.title: Laws ledger — the player-facing surface for enacting/repealing laws (BL-155 companion)
items.summary: Filed 2026-07-19 (design session, Ben) as the UI companion BL-155 explicitly excludes from its own scope ('no UI... committed - the point is to position the model'). BL-155's design is unusually settled for design-owed - a four-family effect taxonomy and ten named laws already enumerated - but nothing yet names how the player actually SEES or ENACTS a law. Settled 2026-07-19: Budget ledger keeps its own Tax/Wages controls; the Laws ledger shows those two laws read-only alongside the other eight.
items.design:
**Gap.** BL-155 (v0.1.2, Laws & policy surface) settles the law object shape - `condition_set` + polymorphic `effect`, four effect families (margin modifiers, quantity clamps, cost adders, gates), ten named laws, and the determinism seam (`run_economy_step` resolves all active laws' condition-sets at one fixed point) - but is explicitly data-model + stub only, no UI. This item is the missing player-facing half: a place to browse the law list, read what's active, and enact/repeal.

**Shape (matches the existing ledger family).** A new ledger window (`draw_laws_ledger`, alongside `balance_ledger.cpp` / the Market and Construction ledgers), nav-rail toggle per the standing Toggle rule (io-standing-rules.md - re-clicking the active nav icon closes it, doesn't collapse to an overview). Lists the ten BL-155 laws grouped by effect family, each row showing: name, one-line effect description, active/inactive state, and - for conditional laws - the `condition_set` gate in plain language (e.g. a wartime tax reads 'active only during war'). An enact/repeal control per law, gated on the player being able to afford/qualify (exact gate is BL-155's to define; this item only renders + dispatches the toggle).

**The BL-171 reconciliation (settled below).** The Budget ledger already carries stubbed **Tax** and **Wages** tier selectors (`ui_state.budget_tax_tier` / `budget_wage_tier`, drawn, no economic effect) built ahead of BL-155 landing. Two of BL-155's ten laws - **extraction tax** and **labour-contract floor** - are exactly what those stubs anticipate.

**Determinism.** Read-only + a single enact/repeal write per player action, landing on the same tick boundary BL-155's condition-set resolution already uses (laws read the *previous* tick's resolved values, never mid-tick mutating ones per BL-155's determinism seam) - this item adds no new determinism risk beyond what BL-155 itself introduces.

**Sequencing.** Hard-blocked on **BL-155** landing its data model and enforcement seam first - this item is the view over that model, not a parallel track. Natural to promote as the second half of the same v0.1.2 batch rather than a fully separate session.

### Settled 2026-07-19 (Ben)
**Stay separate.** The Budget ledger keeps its own simplified Tax/Wages tier selectors as the fast-path control (`ui_state.budget_tax_tier` / `budget_wage_tier`, wired to real economics once BL-155 lands - that wiring is BL-155's job, not this item's). The Laws ledger lists all ten laws for browsing, but shows **extraction tax** and **labour-contract floor** read-only there (state mirrors the Budget ledger's tiers; enact/repeal for those two happens on the Budget ledger, not here) - the other eight get full enact/repeal controls in the Laws ledger. Two surfaces, one law each is written from exactly one place, so no drift risk despite staying separate.

items.title: Ports / sea trade — coastal-tile shipping as a logistics mode distinct from land routes
items.summary: Filed 2026-07-21 (design session, Ben) as a spin-off of BL-168 — Ben's coastal vision was broader than fishing alone: a port building on coastal tiles enabling sea-based trade routes, a distinct logistics mode from the land road/rail network. Kept out of BL-168's own scope (fishing stays narrow) per Ben's call; design-owed. SETTLED 2026-08-02 (all three): ocean cost is DISTANCE-BASED like BL-153 convoy pricing, never flat — a flat rate makes distance free at sea and breaks BL-191 haul-distance pricing that BL-263 just made load-bearing; sea advantage is a lower per-unit RATE, not a distance exemption. Rivers DO cheapen a port hinterland reach, using BL-170 existing land discount applying where it already would — free, and it makes river-mouth ports outperform open-coast ones, which is what actually happened. A DISTINCT Port building, not a coastal market variant: conflating them makes every coastal market a port and removes the placement decision that is the whole feature, and it keeps one rule (a mode is gated by a building at each endpoint) shared with BL-173 rail depot.
items.design:
**Idea — design owed.** A port building placeable on coastal tiles (using [[BL-168]]'s runtime coastal-adjacency predicate — any of a tile's 6 hex neighbours is ocean) that opens a **sea trade route** mode: convoys travel tile-to-tile over ocean between two ports rather than the land road/rail network. Open questions: how ocean-crossing cost compares to land traversal (a flat rate? distance-based like current convoy pricing, BL-153?); whether it interacts with [[BL-170]]'s river-mouth tiles (a river reaching the coast plausibly cheapens the adjoining port's hinterland reach); whether ports are a distinct building or a coastal variant of the existing market/depot. Sits alongside [[BL-189]] (coastal defense) as the other half of the coastal-identity cluster Ben raised this session. **Post-v0.1.0** — a new logistics mode is a meaningful scope addition beyond the prototype's road/convoy loop; revisit once land logistics (roads, BL-172/173) are stable. Authority → PRODUCTION.md for the building, SUPPLY.md for the trade-route mode. Ben design session 2026-07-21.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the three questions

**1. Ocean cost is DISTANCE-BASED, matching convoy pricing (BL-153). Not a flat rate.**

A flat ocean rate would make distance free at sea, and that is not a small inconsistency — it
breaks BL-191's haul-distance pricing, which BL-263 has just made load-bearing for every
outpost market's opening prices. A world where hauling by land costs by distance and hauling by
sea does not would be arbitraged into nonsense immediately, and correctly so.

Sea's advantage is a **lower per-unit rate**, not a distance exemption. That is what makes it a
mode rather than a loophole.

**2. Rivers DO cheapen a port's hinterland reach — using BL-170's existing discount.**

BL-170 already made rivers a logistics discount on land traversal. A river reaching the coast at
a port means the port's *land leg* inland gets that discount, which is not new machinery — it is
the existing discount applying where it already would. So the answer is yes, and it is free.

Worth stating because it produces the right emergent geography for nothing: river-mouth ports
outperform open-coast ports, which is what actually happened to every major port city.

**3. A distinct Port building, not a coastal market variant.**

Conflating them would make every coastal market automatically a port, which removes the
placement decision entirely — and the placement decision is the whole feature. A market is a
*clearing venue*; a port is a *mode gate*. Different jobs.

It also keeps the pattern consistent with BL-173's rail depot: a transport mode is unlocked by a
building at each endpoint. One rule, two modes, rather than sea being special.

Placement uses BL-168's runtime coastal-adjacency predicate, as the item says.

**Sequence after BL-172/BL-173** (land logistics proven first), unchanged.

items.title: Coastal defense — military-positioning note for coastal tiles (stub, parked)
