items.title: Building selection element - reshape to the tile Selection three-column format
items.summary: Rebuild the building Selection element to follow the tile element's three-column layout. Ben to design. 2026-08-02 sweep: Q5 SETTLED (rival buildings degrade IN PLACE — same three-column skeleton with pages absent rather than blanked, matching how the BL-089 activity fog already degrades content without swapping surfaces) and sequencing SETTLED (now requires BL-265, not just the landed BL-214). Q1-Q4 remain OPEN and are Ben’s by his own written instruction — now stated against measured column widths (135 / 254 / 135 px at the 1280x720 floor, 260 px band height) so he can answer against real numbers per Rule 0b. Q1-Q4 ANSWERED 2026-08-03: Ben delegated them (NR-023 option 3) against the measured widths rather than reserving them further; item is now designed.
items.design:
**Opened for Ben to design, 2026-07-30, at his request:** "another thing to open for me to design is selection of buildings. We do want this to follow the same format as our tile selection."

**DESIGN OWED — do not guess the layout.** Ben designs this one; the tile element's proportions came from his mockup and this is its sibling.

### The reference (what "same format" means)
The tile element (`draw_tile_selection`, BL-123 reshaped BL-213) runs **left to right** in three columns:
1. **Left quarter** — zoomed hex neighbourhood (`draw_tile_neighbourhood`, radius 2), selected tile picked out.
2. **Centre half** — a paged metric **accordion**, one titled graph at a time with a `< Name (i/N) >` pager.
3. **Right quarter** — a **2x3 action button grid** (Construct / Manage / History / Supply + two reserved).

### What the building element is today
`draw_building_selection` is a **vertical stack**, not three columns: output lead ("701.4 Agricultural Produce / tick" + a % of nominal bar + status), a Profitability block (Revenue / Inputs / Wages / Maint / Net), Production method (recipe combo), Workforce (Auto checkbox + target slider + the BL-179 "Body allows 84% (labour short) - habitability 0.40" line), then "On this tile" (stack capacity) and Demolish.

### The open questions for Ben
1. **What occupies the left quarter?** The tile's hex neighbourhood is a natural analogue (the building's surroundings), but the building already has an identity/emblem header. Same render, or something else?
2. **What pages through the centre accordion?** Candidates: output over time, profitability components, workforce history, input-supply adequacy. The tile element pages one graph per deposited resource — the building's equivalent list is not obvious and needs Ben's call.
3. **Where do the two LEVERS go?** Recipe combo and workforce slider are controls, not facts, and the tile element's right quarter is buttons only. Do they take the right column (making it controls rather than actions), or sit under the accordion?
4. **Does the 2x3 action grid apply?** A building's actions are fewer (Manage is redundant when already selected; Demolish is one). What fills six slots?
5. **Rival buildings** show "Competitor building - intel only" under BL-068. How does that degrade in a three-column layout — empty columns, or a distinct narrower form?

Sequence with **BL-214** (drill-through disclosure levels), which decides how much any card shows before asking.

## 2026-08-02 — everything that is not the layout, settled. The layout is STILL Ben's.

Worked during the design-owed sweep. The item's own instruction — "do not guess the layout,
Ben designs this one" — is honoured: questions 1-4 are layout and are **left open**, now
stated against real measurements so Ben can answer in one pass instead of against prose.
Question 5 is not a layout question and is settled below, as is the sequencing.

**Status stays `design-owed` deliberately.** This is the one item in the v0.1.1 set that did
not flip, and it is not an oversight — the tile element's proportions came from Ben's mockup,
and its sibling should too.

### Q5 SETTLED — rival buildings degrade IN PLACE; there is no second layout

The only question here that follows from the model rather than from taste.

**The rival form is the same three-column skeleton, with columns that lose content, not a
distinct narrower form.** Two reasons, both structural:

1. **It is what the discovery model already does everywhere else.** The activity fog (BL-089)
   has four tiers — Unknown / Known / Stale / Visible — and it degrades *content* while
   keeping the surface. It does not swap in a different panel per tier. A building card that
   changed shape when the owner changed would be the only place in the app where less
   information means a different object.
2. **Two layouts is two layouts.** Every future change to the building element would have to
   be made twice, and the narrow variant would drift — which is the per-surface divergence
   BL-214 existed to end.

Concretely, under BL-068 (rival buildings visible, internals private):

- **Left column** — unchanged. Whatever occupies it for your own buildings is positional or
  contextual, and position is exactly what is visible about a rival.
- **Centre accordion** — pages that read internals (profitability, workforce, recipe) are
  **absent**, not blanked. A page that says "Unknown" for every rival is noise repeated N
  times; the pager's `(i/N)` simply reports a smaller N. Any page computable from public
  market data survives.
- **Right column** — actions degrade to what a non-owner may do. Demolish and any
  lever disappear; a Supply/History view over public data can stay.
- **"Competitor building - intel only"** stays as the header note, which is where a
  one-line status belongs.

If the centre would have **zero** pages for a rival, the accordion shows a single honest
"No public data for this building" page rather than an empty pager. Stated so nobody
discovers it at runtime.

### Sequencing SETTLED — this now depends on BL-265, not just BL-214

The item says "sequence with BL-214", which was right when written; BL-214 has since landed
and **BL-265** (settled 2026-08-02) revised the model on top of it. BL-229 should be built
against BL-265's vocabulary, not BL-214's:

- Two controls, `⌄` expand-in-place and `›` full-canvas, right-gutter aligned.
- A full-canvas accordion shows **every** page scrolled (BL-265 change 3) — which incidentally
  answers part of Q2's worry: the centre column does not have to fit everything, because
  everything is one control away.
- Both glyphs are **drawn**, not typed (BL-234).

`requires` updated to BL-265.

### THE MEASUREMENTS Ben asked to see before answering (Rule 0b)

All derived from the code, not eyeballed. Band rect:
`band_left = shell_column_width(disp_x)`, `right_edge = disp_x - 8 - minimap_width`,
`band_h = minimap_height + 8`.

| | 1280x720 (the floor) | 1920x1080 |
|---|---|---|
| Shell column `W` | 380 px (clamped up from 256) | 384 px |
| Minimap `mm_w` | 336 px | 336 px |
| **Band width** | **556 px** | **1192 px** |
| **Band height** | **260 px** (fixed) | **260 px** (fixed) |
| Content `avail` (less 8 px padding each side) | 540 px | 1176 px |
| **Left quarter** (`0.25 * avail`) | **135 px** | **294 px** |
| **Centre half** (remainder less 2x8 spacing) | **254 px** | **572 px** |
| **Right quarter** (`0.25 * avail`) | **135 px** | **294 px** |
| Usable column height (less padding, header row, separator) | ~212 px | ~212 px |

Band height is **260 px at both**, and stays 260 until the display's *smaller* dimension
exceeds 1200 (`minimap_width` floors at 336).

**The number that matters most: 135 px.** That is what the left and right quarters actually
get at the 1280x720 floor. The tile element's 3x2 action grid lives in 135 x 212 px — about
44 px per button row. That is the real budget any answer to Q1 and Q4 has to fit.

### The four open questions, restated against those numbers

1. **Left quarter (135 x 212 px @1280).** The hex neighbourhood is the natural analogue but the
   building already has an identity/emblem header, so it may be redundant. At 135 px a radius-2
   neighbourhood is ~27 px per hex — legible, but not by much.
2. **Centre accordion pages (254 x 212 px @1280).** Candidates: output over time, profitability
   components, workforce history, input-supply adequacy. Note the tile element derives its page
   *list* from data (one per deposited resource); the building's equivalent list is authored, so
   this is a genuine choice rather than a derivation. BL-265 means the list can be longer than
   the column comfortably shows.
3. **The two levers (recipe combo, workforce slider).** They are controls, not facts, and the
   tile element's right quarter is buttons only. Right column (making it controls rather than
   actions), or under the accordion? A combo box at 135 px is tight; a slider at 135 px is very
   tight.
4. **The 2x3 action grid.** A building's actions are fewer — Manage is redundant when the
   building is already selected, Demolish is one. What fills six slots, or does the grid shrink?

**Ask with the live app open** (standing rule for visual questions), not with these numbers
alone — the table is there so the conversation starts from what is actually on screen.

## Q1–Q4 ANSWERED 2026-08-03 — delegated by Ben (NR-023 option 3)

Ben released his own reservation and delegated the four layout questions, answered here against
the measured column widths above rather than against prose. Recorded as a **delegated** design,
not a Ben mockup — if the built result near-misses the tile element, that is the risk he
accepted, and the fix is his sketch.

### A1 — Left quarter: keep the hex neighbourhood (135 × 212 px)

Same `draw_tile_neighbourhood` render at radius 2 as the tile element, with the building's own
tile picked out and its marker glyph drawn on it. Three reasons:

1. **The sibling claim is the whole item.** "Same format as tile selection" is the brief; a
   different left column breaks precisely the analogy the item exists to create.
2. **It survives the rival case unchanged.** Q5 already settled that position is what is public
   about a rival building — so this is the one column that needs no degradation logic at all.
3. **It answers a real question.** What surrounds a building governs stack capacity, road
   access, and adjacent deposits. That is not decoration.

At 135 px a radius-2 neighbourhood is ~27 px per hex — legible, and *identical to what the tile
element already ships*, so it is a known quantity rather than a new risk. The identity/emblem
stays in the header row, where a one-line identity belongs (and where the "Competitor building —
intel only" note already sits). The **"On this tile" stack-capacity line moves under the left
column**: it is positional information about the tile, which is what this column is about.

### A2 — Centre accordion: four authored pages, ordered symptom → cause (254 × 212 px)

The tile element derives its page list from data; the building's is authored, so the ordering
is a design statement. Order:

1. **Output** — output/tick against nominal, over time. The headline fact, and today's lead.
2. **Profitability** — Revenue / Inputs / Wages / Maintenance / Net, over time.
3. **Input supply** — per-input adequacy. The page that *explains* a bad Output page.
4. **Workforce** — target vs actual vs body-allowed, carrying the BL-179 habitability line.

A player paging left-to-right walks **symptom → consequence → cause**: page 1 says whether it is
working, page 2 says what that is worth, pages 3–4 say why it is not. That ordering is the
reason to author the list rather than pick pages ad hoc.

For a rival, pages 2–4 are internals and are **absent** (not blanked) per Q5; page 1 survives
only where output is publicly inferable, so in practice a rival building will usually show Q5's
single honest "No public data for this building" page.

### A3 — The two levers: under the accordion, not in the right column

The centre half becomes **accordion (~170 px) + a fixed two-row lever strip (~40 px) at its
foot** — recipe combo on row 1, workforce slider + Auto checkbox on row 2, both at the full
254 px, which is workable where 135 px is not.

1. **135 px genuinely does not fit them.** The measurements section says so; a combo is tight
   and a slider is very tight.
2. **It keeps each column's meaning stable across the two siblings.** The right quarter means
   *actions you take*; a recipe combo and a workforce dial are *settings you hold*. Mixing them
   makes the column mean different things in the two elements, which is the drift the format
   claim is trying to prevent.
3. **BL-265 pays for the vertical.** A full-canvas accordion shows every page scrolled, so the
   centre column no longer has to fit everything — borrowing ~40 px of its height is affordable
   in a way it was not before BL-265 landed.

The levers stay **visible at all times** rather than paging away. That is deliberate: they are
the two things a player changes most often, and putting a lever behind a pager is exactly the
micromanagement tax BL-181's auto-dial exists to reduce.

### A4 — Keep the 2×3 action grid; fill four, reserve two

Filled: **Construct** (place another of this type — the most common follow-on action, and the
tile element's own verb), **History**, **Supply**, **Demolish**. **Manage is dropped** — it is
redundant when the building is already selected, as the item itself observed. Two slots stay
reserved.

Keep 2×3 rather than shrinking to 2×2:

1. **The grid geometry is the most visually load-bearing part of the "same format" claim.** A
   2×2 sibling beside a 2×3 reads as a mistake rather than a variation.
2. **Reserved slots already have a home here** — the tile element ships two.
3. **v0.1.x will fill them.** BL-160/161 (exchange policy, counterparty) are plausible
   per-building actions.

**Demolish sits bottom-right** — furthest from the pointer's resting path, because it is the one
destructive verb. It is also the first to disappear for a rival under Q5.

### What is still Ben's

Nothing blocking. If the built result reads wrong beside the tile element, the recourse is the
mockup route (NR-023 option 2) — this design is explicitly the delegated answer, not a claim to
have matched his eye.

items.title: Landform has no visual render — draw the axis the build cost already charges for
items.summary: terrain_colour switches on COMPOSITION ONLY, so six of the seven landforms — mountain, highland, canyon, valley, crater, rift — render as flat hexes indistinguishable from plains, even though landform drives build cost x1.0->x2.0, hazard, habitability and mineral richness. The two-axis model is not thin; the renderer discards half of it, and hex_render.hpp:23 already claims a glyph channel that was never built. Fix is two channels mirroring Pass 5's own structure: a glyph for the three categorical FEATURE CORES (mountain/rift/crater cluster seeds) and an edge/relief channel for the ordinal elevation read, always-on chrome rather than a lens, since the cost multiplier applies whether or not a lens is active. Gated on a landform histogram that does not exist yet — world_audit counts compositions only — because the glyph/relief proportion depends on how sparse feature cores actually are.

items.title: Bridge contiguous landform runs into one spanning marker, not a repeated per-tile glyph
items.summary: BL-231 draws a landform glyph per tile, so a run of three mountains reads as three identical icons rather than as one range. Ben's call on seeing it: bridge contiguous runs into a single SPANNING marker — a wavy ridge threading a line of mountains, a filled interior where a cluster is compact enough that its middle has no exposed edge. The mechanism is already proven 150 lines away in the same file: BL-172's road span/symmetry fix has each roaded tile draw its OWN half of every shared edge, centre to edge-midpoint, so two tiles' halves meet exactly at the midpoint and form one continuous span with no cross-tile state. Applies to the LINEAR landforms (mountain, rift, canyon); crater stays discrete because a basin is a blob, not a line. Gated on a contiguity measurement — if most mountain tiles have no mountain cardinal neighbour, spanning almost never fires and the work does not pay.

items.title: Terrain combat modifiers — grade the binary the history ladder already prices conquest with
items.summary: The history ladder ALREADY prices conquest from terrain — `is_barrier` (history_ladder.cpp:91) is a two-value function feeding barrier_q, which drives fragmentation_q, conquest_cost_q, exit_cost_q and therefore polity_seeds and the nation count. It conflates three different things (defensive ground, attritional ground, and open water) into one boolean, so a mountain and a barren plain score identically and a forest scores nothing. Replace it with graded, composition-aware scalars — terrain_defence and terrain_attrition, pure functions parallel to landform_logistics_cost, with no stored state and no save-format change. This adds NO combat resolution, units or rules (still excluded by TECH_FOUNDATIONS); it refines a generation-time input that already exists, and it is the input BL-224's non-hegemony assertions N4/N5 are written against but cannot currently assert against a binary. Gated on measurement: grading the barrier field WILL move the nation count Ben personally set at 14->43 when BL-221 landed.

items.title: Em-dashes and ≥ render as "?" — the font loads with ImGui's default Latin-1 glyph range
items.summary: src/ui/fonts.cpp calls AddFontFromFileTTF without a GlyphRanges, so ImGui builds its default Latin-1 atlas (U+0020-U+00FF). Every UI string above that range renders as '?' — 26 sites use em-dash (U+2014) and >= (U+2265), including entity_summary.cpp's bare em-dash placeholders, which therefore read as an error rather than as 'no selection'. Found while adding the BL-232 landform tooltip, whose string was kept inside Latin-1 to dodge it. Fix is a glyph range covering the punctuation and maths blocks actually used (the bundled DejaVuSans has the glyphs), then confirm the existing sites render.

items.title: Creeds - one pantheon per cradle-culture in its own tongue, tribal conflict that welds cradles, and the common-tongue globalisation
items.summary: Each agrarian cradle becomes a culture with its own generated phonology and a single pantheon shaped by its land (sea/river/forest/storm chief, war god, door of the dead, forge on ore, sealed oath at the charter cradle). The pantheon temperament drives a tribal-conflict stage: won wars weld cradles and lower fragmentation_q before nation seeding (floored at half - no creed-made hegemon). Generation closes with the 1951 common-tongue line; the record renders in the player language (English for dev), proper names stay native.

items.title: Frame-budget HUD — last/avg/max ms + 1% lows, and what a spike was spent on
items.summary: The first of ROADMAP § v0.1.0's three quality-audit instruments, named there since the cut set was written but never itemised — so the cut gate had no buildable owner. Targets: avg < 8 ms, max < 16.7 ms panning the full Kepler tile grid (15,120 tiles). Filed 2026-07-31 while closing the v0.1.0 cut set; the ROADMAP text is the design.

items.title: Econ-tick scaling instrument — per-tick timing and a growth-shape assertion in econ_stability
items.summary: The second of ROADMAP § v0.1.0's three quality-audit instruments, never itemised. Extends the existing econ_stability harness to print per-tick time and to sweep the bodies x corps axis, asserting the tick cost does not grow faster than linearly. Target: well under 1 ms at prototype scale. Filed 2026-07-31 while closing the v0.1.0 cut set.

items.title: Data-creep instrument — entity/pool/market/convoy counters + RSS over a long run, asserting plateau
items.summary: The third of ROADMAP § v0.1.0's three quality-audit instruments, never itemised. A new harness that runs the real generated world long (100 -> 1000+ ticks) sampling entity/component/pool/market/convoy/route counts plus RSS, and asserts they PLATEAU rather than climb — naming the offending structure when one does not. Filed 2026-07-31 while closing the v0.1.0 cut set.

items.title: Golden bands and visual goldens are platform-dependent — CTest and the visual checks cannot be green on Windows and Linux at once
items.summary: Found 2026-07-31 on the first Linux run of the full suite. ai_skill_harness fails 8 of its golden bands (seeds 1-4; seed 0 passes) while its OWN determinism checks (R0) all pass — same-seed runs are byte-identical on this platform. The visual goldens diverge too (9-57% pixel difference across every script). Both golden sets were blessed on Windows/MSVC, so the suite cannot be green on both toolchains, and the v0.1.0 done-definition's 'headless harnesses green' has no unambiguous meaning until this is settled.

items.title: run_corp_strategic_step rescans every tile per due corp — an O(corps x tiles) term that dominates the tick at scale
items.summary: Found 2026-07-31 by the new BL-250 scaling sweep, which is exactly the class of finding the instrument was built for. The strategic-AI candidate scan walks every tile for every due corp, so econ-tick cost grows as size^1.28 rather than linearly: a rounding error to ~64 corps, about HALF the tick at 256. Well inside budget at prototype scale (0.0018 ms/tick, 555x headroom), so this is not a v0.1.0 blocker — it is the named reason the growth curve bends, filed so it stays visible.
items.design:
FOUND 2026-07-31 by BL-250's scaling sweep, on its first run.

## The measurement

    bodies  corps   min ms    growth
    1       8       0.0035      -- baseline
    2       16      0.0080    2.28x for 2.0x size
    2       32      0.0161    2.00x for 2.0x size
    4       64      0.0393    2.45x for 2.0x size
    4       128     0.0924    2.35x for 2.0x size
    8       256     0.2932    3.17x for 2.0x size

    end to end: 32x size -> 83.1x time  =>  time ~ size^1.28

## The cause

`run_corp_strategic_step` (src/world/corp_ai.cpp, landed with BL-202/BL-203) scans the
full tile set for every corp whose strategic cadence is due. That is an O(corps x tiles)
term sitting inside a loop that is otherwise roughly O(corps). At 8 corps it is invisible;
by 256 corps it is about half the tick.

## Why this is NOT a v0.1.0 blocker

At prototype scale the tick is 0.0018 ms mean — 555x under the 1 ms ROADMAP target — and
the largest world in the sweep (128x prototype) still ticks under 1 ms. Nothing is slow.
The curve simply bends, and the ROADMAP's own wording ("confirm it does not grow faster
than linearly in bodies x corps") makes the bend worth naming rather than shrugging at.

## Shape of the fix, when it is wanted

The scan is recomputing a mostly-static thing per corp. The obvious options, cheapest
first: cache the candidate set per body and invalidate on construction/depletion; or
restrict each corp's scan to tiles on bodies where it has presence; or precompute a
per-body ranked candidate list once per tick and let every due corp read it.

Do NOT do this speculatively. It is filed because the instrument found it, and it should
be actioned when corp counts actually rise — which is a v0.2.0+ concern, not a prototype
one. The sweep now asserts the exponent stays under 1.5, so a regression that makes this
worse trips a test.

items.title: The data-creep instrument never exercises convoys or trade routes — three plateau assertions are vacuous
items.summary: Found 2026-07-31 by the BL-251 harness reporting honestly on its own coverage. Over 1500 ticks of the real generated world, no convoy was ever dispatched, so world.convoys, world.trade_routes and world.body_last_glimpse_tick all sat at 0 for the whole run and their plateau assertions passed VACUOUSLY. trade_route is documented as never-erased (components.hpp), i.e. accumulating by construction — precisely the unbounded-structure shape the instrument exists to catch, and the one structure it currently cannot see.

items.title: The generation screen is a globe you can look around — the world forming, with the charts as extras on top
items.summary: REWRITTEN 2026-08-01 (Ben, NEEDS_REVIEW NR-005). The globe is no longer a small sketch beside the charts — it is the generation screen's PRIMARY view, pannable (clamped so you cannot pass either pole), showing the world forming pass by pass, with the charts demoted to 'interesting mathematical extras on top of an immediate view of what the world will look like'. Pre-world rounds, where no body exists yet, show the solar system's shape instead. Ben asked explicitly to be told if this is hard or has unforeseen problems: the honest answer is that the RENDERING is affordable and the two real risks are (a) how the equirectangular source looks when sampled at high latitude and (b) the per-frame CPU cost once the disc is large enough to be a primary view. Both are settled by a throwaway prototype against the ALREADY-GENERATED world before any wizard work — that sequencing is the item's first task. SETTLED 2026-08-02 (four open calls closed): pan PERSISTS across rounds and resets only on a seed change; the pole treatment is a scheduled pick-from-three after task 1 with ACCEPT as the stated fallback so it cannot stall the item; the pre-world view is deliberately a top-down DIAGRAM (spacing is what those rounds decide, and an oblique view hides it) recorded as such in STARTUP.md; and the demoted charts become BL-265 folded verdict rows — so the charts-first view is not deleted, just one control away. Now requires BL-265. Only Ben-eye question left: charts under the globe vs a right-hand rail, to be tried live, not mocked.
items.design:
REWRITTEN 2026-08-01 (Ben, NEEDS_REVIEW Q&A, resolving NR-005). Supersedes the original 2026-08-01 filing, which framed the globe as a ~200 px sketch beside the charts with interaction explicitly out of scope. The projection design in that version was sound and is kept; what changes is the globe's STATUS on the screen, and the addition of panning and a pre-world view.

## What Ben asked for

"I just think it would be cool to see the world forming as a 3d shape with pan features. E.g. can't go above north pole or below south pole. For pre-world steps, we can show the solar system shape. That way, the expanded details are interesting mathematical extras on top of an immediate view of what the world will look like."

Three changes fall out of that, and the third is the one that reorders the screen:

1. **Pan**, clamped in latitude so the camera never passes either pole. No roll.
2. **A pre-world view.** Early rounds have no body to draw; show the solar system's shape instead, so the screen is never empty and the player always sees the thing being decided.
3. **The globe is the PRIMARY view; the charts are extras.** This is the real change. The wizard today is charts with prose; it becomes a world you look at, with the derivation available on top. The disclosure spine (BL-214) already supplies the fold idiom for exactly that relationship.

## Ben asked to be told if this is hard. Here is the honest read.

### It is not a 3D pipeline, and it must not become an argument for one

The app is ImGui over SDL_Renderer's 2D path — no depth buffer, no shaders — and TECH_FOUNDATIONS forbids swapping that out. None of this needs it, because the globe is drawn as a **per-pixel inverse projection into a texture**, not as projected geometry:

- For each pixel of an NxN disc, invert the orthographic projection to a (lat, lon) on the sphere; skip pixels outside the disc.
- Sample the source field at (lat, lon), shade, write RGBA. Upload once per frame and draw through ImGui's image path.

This is worth stating because the obvious alternative — projecting each tile as a polygon — is the one that breaks. That approach would put ~7,500 front-facing hexes at 6 vertices each against ImGui's 16-bit draw indices (65,535), which works at 90x42 and falls over at 180x84; and it would render polar rows as degenerate slivers, because a row-offset hex grid has no tile that IS the pole. Per-pixel sampling has no vertex budget at all, and the poles merely OVERSAMPLE the top row (smearing) instead of shattering. Do not "optimise" this into geometry.

### Risk 1 — how the poles actually look (the one that cannot be settled on paper)

The source is an equirectangular grid, 180 columns x 84 rows on the home body. Wrapped to a sphere, longitude compresses toward the poles, so the top and bottom rows smear across the cap. Ben's own pan constraint hides the worst of it — a camera that cannot pass the pole never looks straight down at it — but it is visible at high latitude and no amount of design settles whether it reads as "a planet" or "a texture bug".

Possible treatments, none chosen: a shaded ice cap drawn over the top few degrees (cheap, and physically plausible since those rows are polar anyway); latitude-weighted sampling; or simply accepting it.

### Risk 2 — CPU cost, which the ORIGINAL item got backwards

The first version warned that the continents pass was "the expensive half" and might not be affordable per control move. Reading the code says otherwise: `continents.cpp` is 231 lines of O(width x height x plates) work — roughly 180 x 84 x ~12 integer operations for the home body. That is sub-millisecond territory. **The generation half is probably not the cost; the DRAWING half might be.**

A 200 px sketch is ~31k lit pixels per frame. A primary view at 600 px is ~283k, each needing an inverse projection (asin/atan2 or equivalent) plus a sample and a shade. At 60 fps that is the frame's dominant cost and could plausibly run into milliseconds.

The fix is structural rather than clever, and should be designed in from the start: **the pixel -> (lat, lon) mapping depends only on the disc size and the camera LATITUDE**. Rotation is a longitude ADD. So cache a lookup table of per-pixel (lat, lon0) and rebuild it only when the size or the pan latitude changes — spinning then costs one addition and one sample per pixel, and panning costs a rebuild only while the drag is happening.

Measure before assuming either way. The point of stating this is that the cost lives somewhere the first version did not look.

### Risk 3 — the pre-world view is a different object

`solar_system_canvas` exists, but it is a 2D top-down diagram of orbits, not a 3D scene. Dropping it in for the early rounds gives the screen two visual languages: a diagram, then a globe. That may be fine — they genuinely are different things, and a system IS better read from above — but it is a deliberate call, not an oversight, and STARTUP.md should say which it is.

### What is genuinely cheap

- **Pan with a latitude clamp.** Two floats and a clamp; the projection already takes a camera basis.
- **"The world forming."** The per-pass intermediates already exist — `generate_body_tiles` takes an optional `generation_record`, which is the same data GENERATION_LEDGER.md is built on. Showing height, then ocean, then bands, then composition is a matter of choosing which field to sample, not of new generation work.

## Sequencing — the prototype comes first, and not in the wizard

**Task 1: prove the projection against the ALREADY-GENERATED world.** Draw the globe from a live `world`, in a throwaway debug window, on a machine Ben can look at. This puts the pole artifact and the real frame cost in front of him in an afternoon, using data that already exists.

Everything else is contingent on that. If the poles read badly the whole direction changes shape, and any wizard integration built first is wasted. Do not start at the startup flow.

**Task 2 onward** (only after task 1 is seen): the wizard preview chain, the field-per-stage progression, the pan clamp, the solar-system view for pre-world rounds, and the layout inversion that demotes the charts.

## The tier question, revised

The original item proposed two fidelities — a characterisation globe from planetology scalars (Tier 1) and a real-landmass globe that also runs continents plus tile Pass 1 (Tier 2) — and recommended building both. Ben's framing wants the real planet as the immediate view, so **Tier 2 is the target** and Tier 1 survives only for rounds where the landmass genuinely is not decided yet.

That distinction still has to be VISIBLE. A globe showing generic banding in round 1 and real continents in round 3 without saying so teaches the player something false — the same lying-figure objection Ben applied to markets in BL-263. Caption which one is on screen.

## Determinism

Unchanged, and load-bearing. The globe reads generated state and never writes it. Rotation is wall-clock and confined to the shading pass; it must not reach any field the world samples. If the preview runs the continents/height pass, it must be the SAME deterministic pass real generation runs, seeded identically — a globe showing a planet the campaign then does not produce is worse than no globe.

## Open calls

1. **Does pan persist across rounds**, or reset when the preview re-runs? Persisting is friendlier; resetting makes each round's globe comparable.
2. **The pole treatment** — cap, weighted sampling, or accept. Answer after task 1, not before.
3. **Whether the solar-system view is a diagram or a projection.** See risk 3.
4. **Where the charts go** once demoted — folded under the globe, a side rail, or a separate round.

## Not in scope

Any 3D rendering pipeline or renderer change. Zoom, click-through, or selection on the globe. Reuse on the in-game canvases (CANVASES.md owns those; the zoom ladder is settled). Cities, borders, buildings or any post-generation overlay.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the four open calls

Taken in the order the item lists them. Call 2 is settled as a *procedure* rather than an
answer, because the item is right that it cannot be answered on paper — but a scheduled
decision with a stated fallback is settled enough to promote, whereas an open one is not.

### 1. Pan PERSISTS across rounds; it resets only when the SEED changes

The item offered persist (friendlier) versus reset (each round comparable). Persist wins, and
the framing that decides it is the item's own: this is **one world being formed**, not a
sequence of separate globes. A camera that snaps back each time a pass completes makes the
same planet look like a different one every few seconds — the viewer reads a cut, not a
refinement, which undoes the exact thing the globe is for.

The comparability argument is real but is answered better another way: the passes overlay the
**same geometry**, so the player compares by watching a fixed frame change, not by having the
frame re-established for them. Holding the camera still is what makes the comparison possible;
resetting it is what breaks it.

There is also a plainer reason. Pan is a deliberate player action, and silently undoing a
player's action on a timer is the kind of thing that reads as a bug even when it is
intentional.

**Reset when the seed changes** — a new seed is a genuinely different world and there is
nothing to hold the camera on. That is the only reset.

### 2. Pole treatment — a MEASUREMENT with a stated fallback, not a design call

Unchanged in substance: this is answered after task 1, by looking. What is settled is that it
cannot stall the item.

The three candidates are already enumerated (shaded ice cap over the top few degrees;
latitude-weighted sampling; accept it), so Ben's decision is a **pick from three**, not a
fresh design conversation — which is the difference between a scheduled call and an open one.

**Fallback, if the artifact is inconclusive or nobody wants to decide: ACCEPT.** Do nothing.
The pan clamp already hides the worst of it by construction (a camera that cannot pass the
pole never looks straight down at one), and both treatments are purely additive later — a cap
is a shaded overlay on top of a working globe, not a change to the projection. Shipping
"accept" therefore costs nothing but a possible revisit, while blocking on the question costs
the whole item. Choose the treatment if the artifact makes it obvious; otherwise ship and move.

### 3. The solar-system view is a DIAGRAM, deliberately — and STARTUP.md says so

The item flags that using `solar_system_canvas` for pre-world rounds gives the screen two
visual languages, and asks whether that is a call or an oversight. It is a call, and the right
one.

**The two subjects genuinely differ, and the diagram is the better read of its own subject.**
What the pre-world rounds decide is orbits, body count and spacing — and an oblique 3D view of
a solar system *hides* spacing, which is the one thing those rounds are choosing. A top-down
diagram shows it directly. Rendering the system as a perspective scene would be prettier and
strictly less informative, which is the trade the whole item argues against elsewhere (the
lying-figure objection in the tier question).

**It is also nearly free.** `solar_system_canvas.{hpp,cpp}` already exists and already draws
this. Building a second, 3D-ish system view means new code whose only merit is matching a
visual language the globe has not established yet.

**The transition is a feature.** Diagram giving way to globe is the moment the world starts
existing. That is worth reading as an event rather than smoothing away — it marks the same
boundary the tier caption (below) has to state in words anyway.

Record it in STARTUP.md as a deliberate two-language screen with the reason, so the next
reader does not "unify" it.

### 4. The charts fold — BL-265's vocabulary, no new machinery

"Interesting mathematical extras on top of an immediate view" is exactly the relationship the
disclosure spine already models, and BL-265 has just settled the control vocabulary for it. So
the demoted charts need no new disclosure concept at all:

- Each chart rests as a **folded verdict row** — one line saying what it concluded.
- `⌄` expands that chart **in place**, beside the globe, which is the common case.
- `›` takes the **canvas** for it, and per BL-265 change 3 a full-canvas accordion shows
  *every* chart scrolled — which is the old charts-first screen, now available on demand
  rather than imposed.

That last point is worth stating plainly: **demoting the charts does not remove the
charts-first view, it puts it one control away.** The item is a re-ranking of defaults, not a
deletion, and framing it that way should defuse any worry about losing the derivation.

**Adds a dependency on BL-265** (disclosure controls revision), which supplies `⌄`/`›` and the
right-gutter rule. Without it this item would have to invent its own expander, which is the
per-surface reinvention BL-214 existed to end.

**Left for Ben's eye, and only this:** whether the folded chart rows sit **under** the globe or
in a **right-hand rail** beside it. Both work with the fold idiom, the difference is only which
one keeps the globe largest at 1280x720, and it is a five-minute experiment once the globe
renders — not a paragraph. Ask with the live app open (both variants built), not with a
mockup.

### Sequencing is unchanged and still load-bearing

Task 1 (prove the projection against the already-generated world, in a throwaway debug window)
comes first and everything else is contingent on it. None of the four settlements above
weakens that — call 2 explicitly depends on it, and calls 1/3/4 are cheap to honour whatever
the prototype shows.

## Task 1 ruled done 2026-08-09 (NR-089, Ben)

The wizard preview pane landed 2026-08-08 (BL-319) — a hex-sampled orthographic globe of the actual generated surface, byte-parity verified against make_hard_coded_world — is ruled to BE this item's task-1 projection proof, promoted from the planned throwaway debug window into the real wizard. Remaining slice: player-controlled pan with pole clamp, the measured pole-treatment call (cap / weighted-sampling / accept), the pre-world solar-system diagram stage, and folding the demoted charts through BL-265's disclosure vocabulary in place of the fixed 1/3:2/3 split.

items.title: Body names are generated, and body identity stops being a display string
items.summary: Ben's call, 2026-08-01: planet names should look random rather than fixed, so the solar system reads as generated rather than authored. Today the five bodies carry hard-coded string literals (Helios, Cinder, Kepler, Selene) in hard_coded_world.cpp. The feature is small; the hazard under it is not — several places use the NAME as an identity test, so randomising names silently breaks them.
items.design:
## Two halves, and the second one is load-bearing

### Half 1 (the hazard) — identity must stop being a display string

Randomising names without this is a silent correctness bug, not a cosmetic change. Known sites that compare a body name as identity:

- `src/world/hard_coded_world.cpp:256` — `if (be.name != "Kepler") continue;`
- `tools/verify/history_ladder_harness.cpp:140,141,236`
- `tools/verify/creeds_harness.cpp:135,136`

`world.home_body` already holds the homeworld entity id (`hard_coded_world.cpp:189`), so the homeworld case has a correct answer available today and simply is not used. Replace every name comparison with the entity id — or, where a harness needs "the tiled body" rather than "the home body" specifically, with an explicit role/flag on the body rather than a second name test.

**Do this half first and independently.** It is a strict improvement with or without generated names, and it means the naming change cannot introduce a regression. Re-survey with `grep -rn '.name *[=!]= *"' src/ tools/` before starting; the list above is from 2026-08-01 and filed prose goes stale.

### Half 2 — the name pool

`src/world/city_names.{hpp,cpp}` is the existing model and should be followed rather than reinvented: a deterministic pick from a curated pool, seeded, with no repeats within a world. Bodies want the same shape in `src/world/body_names.{hpp,cpp}`.

Constraints that make the result read as a real system rather than a shuffle:

- **Deterministic from the world seed.** Same seed, same names — this is the standing invariant, and the goldens depend on it.
- **No duplicates within a system**, including moons.
- **Moons should read as moons.** A moon of a named planet wants either a related name or a positional suffix; a moon drawn from the same flat pool as planets makes the system read as a bag of words.
- **Register/tone. SETTLED 2026-08-01 (Ben, NEEDS_REVIEW NR-006): a DELIBERATE MIX, governed by a rule.** Not one register for everything, and not a random draw across three. The registers stay — mythological, descriptive, scientist-eponym — but which one a body gets is DECIDED by what the body is, so the mixing is legible rather than noisy. Ben: "a deliberate mix is great."

  The reason this beats a single register: a rule the player can half-perceive reads as a world with a HISTORY of being named — different bodies named by different people for different reasons, which is what a real catalogue looks like — where one uniform register reads as a generator. The player never has to articulate the rule for it to work; they only have to sense that the names are not arbitrary.

  **The rule itself is the residual call and is NOT settled.** Proposed, for Ben to accept or replace at promotion: planets take the MYTHOLOGICAL register (named first, from a distance, by people who could only see lights); moons take DESCRIPTIVE names (named later, close up, by whoever surveyed them); and the SCIENTIST-EPONYM register is reserved for whatever was catalogued rather than observed — which today would be the home body, Kepler, and would explain why it is the odd one out rather than making it an inconsistency to fix. Whatever rule is chosen, write it into the doc so a later session extending the pool extends it the same way; an unstated rule decays into the noise it was meant to prevent.

## Verification

`world_audit` and the determinism harnesses must stay green — this touches world generation, so a same-seed regeneration must produce identical names, and the harnesses that previously found bodies by name must find them by id. `history_ladder_harness` and `creeds_harness` both need updating as part of the change, not after it.

## Not in scope

Renaming nations, cities or corporations (city names already have their own generator). Player-editable body names. Any change to how many bodies exist — the count knob is fixed at 5 and phased to a later update (STARTUP.md).

items.title: econ_stability's absolute tick bound cannot hold in a Debug build, so the Windows tree is permanently one test red
items.summary: Found 2026-08-01 by the v0.1.0 integrating ctest run. econ_stability fails one assertion on Windows — R6's absolute 1 ms bound at the largest swept rung (128x prototype) — while R5, the growth exponent, the doubling check and finiteness all pass, and the same assertion passes on Linux/Release. The Windows build/ tree is deliberately CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug, so an absolute wall-clock bound measured at -O0 is meaningless. BL-255 fixed the adjacent case (build type UNSET); this one is build type deliberately CHOSEN, and needs the assertion gated on an optimised build rather than widened.

items.title: Every UI element declares its question in a JSON justification store, tied to the backlog item that demanded it
items.summary: Ben's overturn of BL-247's optional-pair settlement (NR-010), plus his correction that the log is DEVELOPMENT documentation and must not appear in-game (NR-018). SETTLED 2026-08-02: every information surface declares the question it answers and why, as an entry in a docs/development/UX_QUESTIONS.{json,md} pair — canonical JSON plus a generated mirror, matching backlog.json/BACKLOG.md — with each entry carrying the id of the backlog item that demanded the surface, which makes it a provenance index in both directions. No audit tool ('the docs are the audit') and no src/ change: the in-game draw path was already removed. The 22 authored pairs seed it from commit d143aa4; thirteen further surfaces have never had one and are the real work.
items.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-01 (Ben, during the NEEDS_REVIEW Q&A pass — see NR-010).

## Where this came from

BL-247 (chart question log) landed with three questions left "open for the promoting session". One was answered without Ben: is a question/why pair REQUIRED on every chart, or optional with a missing pair simply drawing no toggle? The promoting session chose OPTIONAL, so the log is advisory, and recommended a report-only verify pass as a middle road.

Ben overturned both (2026-08-01): "we need to have documentation for each element. For development, I think it's a low storage cost for perpetual clarity. So the docs are the audit, we don't need an audit method or arbitrary resolution."

So: the pair is REQUIRED; enforcement is authorship, not machinery; and NO headless or report-only audit check is to be built. A surface without a justification is a defect a human notices by reading the store, which is the point of the store existing.

## The three changes this makes to BL-247 as landed

1. **Required, not optional.** Every information surface carries a question/why pair.
2. **Every ELEMENT, not every chart.** Ben confirmed the wider reading explicitly: not only things that plot. A table, a ledger, a roll-up card and a panel each answer a question, and each must state it. This is the scope expansion — BL-247's file scope named charts.cpp / generation_charts.cpp / selection_panel.cpp.
3. **The justification moves OUT of the call site into JSON**, and carries the id of the backlog item that demanded the surface. Today the strings are C++ literals passed to `why_note(ui, answers, because)`.

## The provenance requirement (Ben's addition)

"it's going to be important to tie each justification to the backlog item which demanded it."

This is the part that makes the store more than relocated text. With a `backlog_item` on every entry the log becomes a queryable provenance index in both directions:

- Surface -> item: why does this exist, and what asked for it.
- Item -> surface: what did this item actually put on screen.

It also exposes the two gaps neither backlog.json nor user_stories.json can currently show: a surface no item ever demanded (unjustified UI), and an item that claims a UI outcome but owns no surface. That is the same coverage argument USER_STORIES.md makes on the intent axis, applied to the surface axis.

## OPEN — the file shape (Ben has not chosen; do not guess)

Ben wrote "in its own .json file", which has two readings:

- **A — one store.** `docs/ui/question_log.json`, entries keyed by element id, each with `answers` / `because` / `backlog_item` / `files`. Consistent with backlog.json / user_stories.json / requirements.json, and a coverage query is one read.
- **B — one file per element.** `docs/ui/questions/<element>.json`. The literal reading; diffs stay local to the element, but a coverage query walks a directory.

Recommended A on consistency with the existing stores, but this is Ben's call and the item must not be promoted before he makes it.

## OPEN — the load seam

`why_note` takes `const char*`. If the strings live in JSON there are two ways in, and this needs a call rather than a default:

- **Codegen at build time** — a generated header of string literals. Keeps the runtime free of file IO and a missing entry is a BUILD failure, which is the strongest form of "the docs are the audit" that does not require a separate check. Costs a build step.
- **Runtime load** — parse the store at startup, look up by element id. Simpler build, but a missing entry becomes a silent empty note at runtime, which is exactly the failure the required-pair rule exists to prevent.

Codegen is the better fit for Ben's stated position, precisely because it makes the omission loud without adding an audit tool.

## The backfill roster (measured 2026-08-01)

Pairs exist today on three surfaces only — `generation_charts.cpp` (the wizard chart rows), `corporation_dashboard.cpp` (4 roll-up cards) and `selection_card.cpp` (2).

Carrying NO pair: `market_ledger.cpp`, `economy_panel.cpp`, `balance_ledger.cpp`, `tile_inspector.cpp`, `construction_panel.cpp`, `tech_tree_panel.cpp`, `profile_panel.cpp`, `chat_panel.cpp`, `header_panel.cpp`, `hover_card.cpp`, `nav_pane.cpp`, `entity_summary.cpp`, `selection_panel.cpp`.

The roster is the real cost of this item, and the writing is Ben's rather than an implementer's: authoring the pair IS the design check BL-247 named. An implementer can build the store, the seam and the migration of the 11 existing pairs; the backfill text for a surface should be drafted for Ben to accept or rewrite, not invented and left.

## Not in scope

- Any audit/lint/verify check over the store. Explicitly rejected by Ben — the docs are the audit.
- Changing what `why_note` DRAWS (closed-by-default toggle, one note at a time, reset on expand/fold). That behaviour landed with BL-247 and is unchanged here.
- The player-facing wording standard. "Answers" is a real question a player would ask; "Because" is one plain sentence. Also unchanged.

## LATER THE SAME DAY — the log is DEVELOPMENT documentation, not a player surface (NR-018)

Ben, 2026-08-01: "the why shouldn't leak into the UI, players don't need us telling them what they ought to ask of the game."

This retires the PLAYER-FACING half of BL-247. That item had a dual audience — a closed-by-default in-game toggle, and Ben reading the log while designing. Only the second survives. It is a continuation of BL-247's own objection rather than a reversal of it: BL-247 already refused to curate which questions matter; this refuses to state the question in-game at all.

Consequences:

- **The load seam question above is largely MOOT.** If nothing renders in a player build, no codegen and no runtime load into the UI is required. The store is a documentation artifact read by humans and tooling. Keep the codegen option on the table ONLY if NR-018 lands on the development-gated reading.
- **The eleven live `why_note` call sites** (generation_charts, corporation_dashboard, selection_card) and the toggle in detail_level.cpp either come out or go behind a development-only gate. NR-018 carries that call and it is NOT settled.
- **LAYOUT.md must record the supersession.** BL-247's authority text describes a player-facing affordance; the toggle must not just quietly vanish from the app with the doc still promising it.
- **The wording standard changes audience.** "Answers" no longer has to be phrased as a question a player would ask; it is a question the DESIGNER asks of the surface. Warmer, less careful phrasing is fine — nobody is reading it in-game.

This also removes the last reason to prefer any particular draw-helper location — see NR-011, kept but moot.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the store is a UX_QUESTIONS pair, and there is no code

Ben: "Just use the .md and .json structure. We can keep a UX_QUESTIONS pair of files."

So option A, in the project's existing shape:

- **`docs/development/UX_QUESTIONS.json`** — canonical. One entry per information surface.
- **`docs/development/UX_QUESTIONS.md`** — the readable mirror, GENERATED, never hand-edited.

This closes both questions that were open. The file shape is one store, matching `backlog.json`/`BACKLOG.md` and `user_stories.json`/`USER_STORIES.md`. The load-seam question is **void**: NR-018 removed the in-game draw path entirely, so nothing loads these strings at runtime and no codegen is needed. This item now touches NO `src/` file at all — it is a documentation artifact and a renderer.

### Entry shape

Follow the sibling stores rather than inventing fields. Per entry:

- `id` — a stable slug for the surface (e.g. `corp_rollup_production`).
- `surface` — where it lives, in human terms.
- `answers` — the question this surface answers, phrased as a real question.
- `because` — one plain sentence on why this evidence settles it.
- `backlog_item` — **the id of the item that demanded the surface.** Ben's requirement, and the thing that makes this a provenance index rather than relocated prose.
- `files` — the TU(s) that draw it.

### The renderer

`tools/session/render_ux_questions.js`, modelled on `tools/session/render_needs_review.js` (written 2026-08-02, same session, same reason). A mirror kept by hand drifts the moment a pass edits entries in bulk, and a stale mirror is worse than none because it still reads as authoritative.

### Seeding it

The 22 pairs authored for BL-247 are the seed and are recoverable wholesale from commit **d143aa4** — `generation_charts.cpp` (16 chart rows), `corporation_dashboard.cpp` (4 roll-up cards), `selection_card.cpp` (2 tile metrics). They were deliberately NOT harvested into a file at removal time, because doing so would have pre-decided this question.

### The backfill is still the bulk of the work

Thirteen surfaces have never had a pair: `market_ledger`, `economy_panel`, `balance_ledger`, `tile_inspector`, `construction_panel`, `tech_tree_panel`, `profile_panel`, `chat_panel`, `header_panel`, `hover_card`, `nav_pane`, `entity_summary`, `selection_panel`. Draft each for Ben to accept or rewrite — authoring the pair IS the design check, so an invented one that nobody reads defeats the purpose.

### Audience note, now that nothing renders

`answers` no longer has to be phrased as a question a PLAYER would ask; the reader is the designer. Plainer, blunter phrasing is fine — and a surface whose honest entry is "nothing, really" has just told you something.

items.title: Alerts — an enumerable roster of conditions demanding the player's attention (parked until an AI can play the game)
items.summary: MENU.md named an ALERTS roll-up that BL-248 retired by omission; red verdicts on the four cards give the same signal but cannot be enumerated. Ben confirmed alerts are wanted and DEFERRED them deliberately (NR-012, 2026-08-01): where they live and what earns one cannot be decided until the v0.2.0 AI opponent produces play data. Parked — do not promote early. SETTLED 2026-08-02 without unparking: the deferral stands (evidence, not cheapness), but the CRITERION the post-AI evaluation will apply is now settled, turning the wait into a prepared question. An alert must cover what NO card shows — if a condition is already a red verdict on a roll-up it does not earn one, because repetition is how an alert channel becomes ignored. It qualifies only if OFF-SCREEN (true somewhere the player is not looking — probably the main case, since cards describe the whole position but canvases show one place), TIME-CRITICAL, or CROSS-CUTTING. Notably all three MVP candidates (idle building, unsold output, negative cashflow) FAIL this test now that BL-248 cards show them — evidence the roster must be rebuilt from play, not inherited from MENU.md. Also settled as a trap rather than a preference: an alert tracks a CONDITION and clears when it clears, so it is not dismissible as a message — you fix it or mute the class, never the instance.
items.design:
DEFERRED ON PURPOSE 2026-08-01 (Ben, during the NEEDS_REVIEW Q&A pass — see NR-012).

## Where this came from

MENU.md's Slot 1 MVP originally named ALERTS as one of four roll-ups — idle buildings, unsold output, negative cashflow — and noted in passing that it introduces an "alert" concept the game does not otherwise have.

Ben's 2026-07-31 call replaced that MVP four with the exemplar's Production / Trade / Workforce / Finance. The promoting session did NOT reintroduce alerts anywhere, so the concept was retired by omission: an idle building and a negative net now read as red verdicts on their own cards instead.

Ben, asked about it directly (2026-08-01): "We can make alerts. I'm not sure where to put them yet, I think we should just defer this item. There's not much info on how the game plays yet, and I'm saving that eval until after we get basic AI which can play the game."

## Why it is parked rather than designed

The open question is not WHETHER alerts exist but WHERE they live and WHAT earns one, and neither can be answered from the current build. Ben's reason is a real methodological one and worth preserving: the game has no opponent, so nobody knows yet which conditions actually surprise a player mid-campaign. An alert roster designed against a world where nothing competes with you would enumerate the wrong things.

So this unparks after the v0.2.0 AI opponent can play the game, when there is play data to read. Do not promote it earlier on the grounds that it is cheap — cheapness is not the constraint here, evidence is.

## What is settled

- Alerts ARE wanted. This is a deferral, not a rejection.
- The current red-verdict treatment stands in the meantime, and is not a placeholder to be apologised for: a red Finance card IS the signal, it simply cannot be enumerated.

## What is open

- **Where they live.** A dedicated dashboard card, a header strip, the comms dock, or a surface that does not exist yet. MENU.md's original placement was a Slot 1 card; that placement is no longer assumed.
- **What earns one.** The MVP named three (idle building, unsold output, negative cashflow). Whether those are the right three is exactly what the post-AI evaluation decides.
- **Whether an alert is dismissible, and whether it persists across ticks.** Untouched.
- **The relationship to red verdicts.** If a card already shows red, an alert repeating it is noise. The alert concept probably has to earn its place by covering what NO card shows — which is an argument for defining it against play, not against the current surfaces.

## Not in scope

Changing the four roll-up cards, which landed with BL-248 and are Ben's chosen set.

## SETTLED 2026-08-02 — the deferral is honoured; what is settled is the CRITERION the later evaluation applies

Ben's reason for parking this is methodological and correct: nobody knows which conditions
surprise a player until something competes with them. That stands, and this item does **not**
unpark.

What can be settled without play data is the **test** the post-AI evaluation will apply — which
turns the wait into a prepared question rather than an open one.

### The criterion: an alert must cover what NO card shows

The item half-states this ("probably has to earn its place by covering what no card shows");
making it the rule.

**If a condition is already visible as a red verdict on a roll-up card, it does not earn an
alert.** Repeating it is noise, and noise is how alert systems become ignored — at which point
they are worse than absent, because the player has learned to dismiss the channel that was
supposed to carry the urgent thing.

An alert earns its place only if the condition is at least one of:

1. **Off-screen** — true on a body or a surface the player is not currently looking at. This is
   the strongest case and probably the main one, since the roll-up cards describe the player's
   whole position but the canvases show one place at a time.
2. **Time-critical** — acting late is materially worse than acting now. A slowly worsening
   margin is a card; a convoy about to arrive at a market that has gone dormant is an alert.
3. **Cross-cutting** — no single card owns it, because it is a relationship between things
   (a supply chain broken across two bodies).

Notably, all three of the MVP's original candidates — idle building, unsold output, negative
cashflow — **fail this test as stated**, because BL-248's cards now show exactly those. That is
not an argument that alerts are unwanted; it is the evidence that the roster has to be
rebuilt from play rather than inherited from MENU.md.

### One more thing settled, because it is a trap rather than a preference

**An alert tracks a CONDITION, not a message. It clears when the condition clears.**

So it is not "dismissible" in the message sense. Dismissing an alert for a problem that is still
true is the failure mode every alert system eventually has, and it is designed out here rather
than discovered: there is nothing to dismiss, because the alert *is* the condition being true.

If the player wants to stop seeing one, they fix it or they mute that alert *class* — a
deliberate, remembered choice — never that instance.

### Unchanged

Still parked. Unparks after the v0.2.0 AI opponent can play the game, on Ben's stated reasoning
(evidence, not cheapness). BL-248's four roll-up cards stay untouched.

items.title: A scoring system — how the player knows whether they are ahead, on what axis, and against whom
items.summary: Opened by Ben 2026-08-01 (NEEDS_REVIEW Q&A): 'vital for a sprint, we didn't design it yet.' Nothing today tells the player how they compare to anyone else. Two constraints already bind any answer: CONCEPT.md forbids an end-game score (falling behind is progressive, so the measure must be a STANDING, not a verdict), and DISCOVERY.md makes rival internals private (so a score over every corp's true balance hands the player information the intelligence model withholds). Absorbs the restored all-corporations table (NR-012), which asks the right question with the wrong content. Six open calls enumerated; none guessed. PROPOSED 2026-08-02 (NR-022, for Ben to ratify): one interlocking answer to all six calls — a coarse publicly-published PROFILE of four actor-agnostic axes (reach / production / capital / market share, NO total ever), computed from VISIBLE information (ground truth would make the two fogs decorative), published diegetically by the market so rivals show as BANDS while your own figures stay exact, scoring corporations on axes that survive the BL-094 nation pivot, meaningful only within a campaign (no leaderboard), feeding credit terms (BL-073) and counterparty routing (BL-037) but deliberately NOT unified with BL-202 AI utility (Goodhart).
items.design:
DESIGN OWED — opened 2026-08-01 (Ben, NEEDS_REVIEW Q&A pass). NOTHING BELOW IS SETTLED. This item states the question, the constraints the existing corpus already imposes on any answer, and the calls Ben has to make. It deliberately does not propose a formula.

## Why it exists

Ben, 2026-08-01: "Open a new item on a scoring system. This is vital for a sprint, we didn't design it yet." Raised while resolving NR-012 — he first said to merge the restored all-corporations balance table INTO the scoring item, then found no such item existed. So the table is this item's first known surface, not a separate concern.

## The actual question

How does a player know whether they are winning?

Today the honest answer is: they cannot. The player can read their own balance, their own buildings and their own runway. Nothing tells them how that compares to anyone else, or whether a rising balance is a good balance for this point in a campaign. The one surface that ever compared corporations was a two-column balance table, and BL-248 deleted it as a duplicate.

## The constraint that shapes every answer: there is no end-game screen

CONCEPT.md is explicit — "There is no end-game screen. You don't 'lose' an Era; you enter the next one underprepared, and it is hard... falling behind is progressive, not a single failure state."

So this is NOT a victory score. A single scalar that resolves at the end of a campaign is the wrong shape for a game whose stated failure mode is gradual. What the game needs is a STANDING measure — am I ahead or behind, on what axis, right now, and is the gap opening or closing.

That reframing matters more than the formula. A score you can only read at the end teaches nothing; a standing that moves each tick is a feedback signal the player can act on, which is what "stagnation as loss" requires to be legible at all.

## The constraint that limits what can be scored: rival internals are PRIVATE

DISCOVERY.md § competitor visibility (BL-068) settles that rival buildings are visible, rival internals are private, and markets are public. The activity fog (BL-089) further gates what the player knows about a body at all.

This is the sharpest constraint on the item, and the one most likely to be violated by accident: a score computed from every corporation's true balance is information the player is NOT entitled to. The restored corporations table shows exactly that — every rival's balance, exact, unconditionally. It predates the intelligence model.

So any scoring surface has to answer: is the score computed from what the player can SEE, or from ground truth? A visible-information score is honest and makes intelligence valuable; a ground-truth score is simpler and quietly makes BL-068/BL-089 decorative.

## The constraint on the AI side: a score is an objective function

BL-202 landed a deterministic scored-utility layer for corp AI, and the standing rules bound what background corporations may do. If the player-facing score and the AI's utility score are the SAME quantity, the AI is optimising exactly what the player is measured on — which is either elegant or a Goodhart trap, depending on how coarse the measure is. If they are DIFFERENT quantities, the game measures the player on something no opponent is trying to win. Both readings are defensible; the item must not leave this implicit.

## Open calls — Ben's, all of them

1. **WHO is scored.** Corporations only (the player's peers), nations, or both on separate axes. The prototype's player is a corporation; BL-094 pivots the player to a nation at v0.2.0, so a corporation-only design has a known expiry.
2. **ONE number or a PROFILE.** A single standing is legible and comparable; a profile (reach / production / capital / market share) matches a 4X where players win differently and refuses to imply a single race. The profile reading fits CONCEPT's "corner a market and win early WITHIN an Era" better than a scalar does.
3. **DIEGETIC or META.** Is the score something the world produces — a published ranking, a trade-press table, a credit rating other actors react to — or an out-of-world readout for the player alone? A diegetic score can feed mechanics (credit terms, counterparty preference via BL-037) and is the more characterful option; a meta score cannot be gamed by the fiction and is far cheaper.
4. **VISIBLE-INFORMATION or GROUND-TRUTH inputs.** See the privacy constraint above.
5. **What it FEEDS.** A number nobody reacts to is chrome. Candidates: BL-261 (alerts), the AI's target selection, credit/interest terms (FINANCE.md), nation sentiment (BL-225).
6. **Whether it is comparable ACROSS seeds.** A score that means the same thing on a rich and a poor world requires normalisation against what the world could support; one that does not is only readable within a campaign. This decides whether the number can ever be a leaderboard or is strictly a standing.

## What this item absorbs

**The all-corporations table (NR-012).** Restored 2026-08-01 after BL-248 deleted it, and provisionally parked on nav slot 8 (Diplomacy) with its own flag `show_corporations_table`. It is the rough first draft of this item's surface — the right question (how does each corporation compare) with the wrong content (raw private balances, two columns, no context). Do not treat it as an independent surface to polish: it either becomes this item's comparison view or it is retired BY this item, and either way its home moves off slot 8.

## Determinism

Whatever the formula, it is simulation-visible and must be deterministic: integer/fixed-point accumulation, an explicit tie-break, and no iteration over unordered containers without a sorted walk. The same rule BL-222's first-industrialiser argmax carries.

## Read before promoting

docs/CONCEPT.md § How an Era ends (no end-game screen; stagnation as loss), docs/ui/DISCOVERY.md § competitor visibility, docs/economy/FINANCE.md, src/world/corp_ai.hpp (BL-202's utility layer), and BL-094 (the v0.2.0 nation pivot, which decides whether a corporation-only score has a future).

## PROPOSED 2026-08-02 — one coherent answer to all six calls, for Ben to ratify or overturn

The item says the calls are Ben's, all of them, and that stands — this section does not
overrule it. What it does is refuse to leave six blanks, because the six are **not
independent**: answering call 4 very nearly forces call 3, which shapes call 2, which
dissolves call 1's stated expiry. Six separate questions have a combinatorial answer space;
one interlocking package can actually be judged. Recorded as a decision-taken (NR-022) so it
is overturnable rather than quietly becoming precedent.

The shape, in one sentence: **a coarse, publicly-published PROFILE of four axes, computed from
information the player is entitled to see, feeding credit and counterparty terms, meaningful
only within a campaign.**

### Call 4 first — VISIBLE INFORMATION. This one is nearly forced.

Taking it first because it constrains the rest. The item states the risk exactly: a score over
every corporation's true balance "quietly makes BL-068/BL-089 decorative". That is not a close
trade. Discovery is a designed pillar with its own authority doc, two independent fogs and a
body-level visibility tier; a scoreboard reading ground truth would hand the player, for free
and continuously, the precise thing the entire intelligence model is built to meter.

Ground truth is simpler. It is simpler the way deleting the fog is simpler.

**The objection, answered.** A visible-information score is mostly *unknown* in the early game,
when the player has few routes and little presence. That reads as a defect and is actually the
best property of the design: **not knowing where you stand is itself the signal that you have
not invested in knowing.** It gives intelligence a payoff the player can feel (the standing
sharpens as your commercial sphere grows), and it makes the fog a thing you play against
rather than a thing you wait out. A score fully legible on turn one has nothing left to reveal.

### Call 3 — DIEGETIC, because call 4 demands a source

Once the score is computed from public information, it needs somewhere public to be computed.
"The player privately aggregates what they happen to know" is incoherent as a comparison —
comparisons need a common basis.

**So the world publishes it.** DISCOVERY.md already settles that *markets are public*, which is
exactly the substrate a published ranking may legitimately aggregate: traded volumes, cleared
prices, delivered tonnage, visible holdings. A trade-press table / exchange standing / credit
rating is a diegetic object that can honestly exist in 1960 and can honestly see only what the
market saw.

This also resolves the privacy tension rather than dodging it, by splitting resolution:

- **Your own figures: exact.** You read your balance to the credit.
- **Everyone else's: banded.** A rating, a rank, a coarse tier — never a number.

That is how real ratings work, it is trivially cheaper to compute than an exact rival figure,
and it is honest about what an outside observer could know. It also means the surface can show
every corporation without lying, which the restored table (NR-012) could not.

Ben's standing preference for the deeper option over the cheaper one is a factor here and is
named rather than assumed — meta is genuinely less work, and this recommends against it.

### Call 2 — a PROFILE of four axes, not one number

The item already argues this fits a 4X where players win differently, and CONCEPT's "corner a
market and win early within an Era" is a *narrow* victory a scalar would average away. Two
further reasons:

1. **A scalar implies a race with one finish line, which is precisely the end-game framing
   CONCEPT forbids.** A profile cannot be read as a verdict because there is no single thing to
   be ahead on. The shape of the measure enforces the design constraint by construction,
   instead of relying on nobody adding a total later.
2. **A profile degrades gracefully under partial information.** Under call 4 the player will
   often know a rival's market share and not their capital. A profile shows three axes and a
   gap; a scalar would need to fabricate the missing term or refuse to display.

Proposed axes — deliberately four, deliberately public-observable:

- **Reach** — bodies and markets you are present in.
- **Production** — physical output delivered, by volume.
- **Capital** — banded rating, not a balance.
- **Market share** — share of cleared volume in the goods you trade.

**No aggregate row. No total. Ever.** State it in the item, because a total is the single
change that would convert this back into the victory score CONCEPT rules out, and it is the
change someone will propose as a convenience.

### Call 1 — CORPORATIONS now, and the stated expiry dissolves

The item worries a corporation-only design has a known expiry at BL-094 (the v0.2.0 nation
pivot). It does — but only if the axes are corporation-shaped. All four above are
**actor-agnostic**: a nation has reach, production, capital standing and market share in
exactly the same senses.

**So score CORPORATIONS as the scored actor now, with axes that survive the pivot**, and BL-094
changes who appears in the table, not what the table measures. That is a cheap property to have
and an expensive one to retrofit, which is the whole reason to name it at design time.

Nations are not scored in the prototype — they are the saturated background substrate
(GENERATION_STRATEGY.md's economic premise), not competitors, and ranking them against the
player would misdescribe the game being played.

### Call 6 — WITHIN a campaign only. Not comparable across seeds.

Normalising against what a world *could* support would require a total-potential figure that is
(a) expensive to compute, (b) itself private information under call 4, and (c) meaningless
under CONCEPT's no-end-game framing — there is no context in which two campaigns get compared.

A standing is relative to the rivals on *this* world. That is what "am I ahead, and is the gap
opening" needs and it needs nothing more. **This forecloses a leaderboard**, which nothing has
asked for and which the no-end-game rule would have made incoherent anyway.

### Call 5 — it feeds CREDIT and COUNTERPARTY terms, and is NOT the AI's utility function

A number nobody reacts to is chrome, and the diegetic choice earns its extra cost only if the
world acts on it. Two hooks already exist and need no new system:

- **Credit terms.** FINANCE.md's debt interest (BL-073) currently has no risk input. A capital
  standing is exactly a risk input, and "your rating slipped so your borrowing got dearer" is a
  consequence the player can feel and act on.
- **Counterparty preference.** BL-037's preferred-seller routing already picks between sellers.
  Standing is a legitimate tiebreak, and it makes reputation mechanical.

**Kept separate from BL-202's AI utility, deliberately** — the item asks that this not be left
implicit. They are different quantities and must stay so:

- BL-202's utility is an **internal optimiser over ground truth**; the corp AI knows its own
  books exactly.
- The standing is a **coarse public view** built from what the market saw.

If they were unified, every AI would be directly optimising the published number, which is the
Goodhart trap the item names — and worse, it would require the AI to read a public aggregate it
has no reason to care about. Different quantities is both the safer answer and the more truthful
one. The AI may *read* standing as one input to target selection (who is worth competing
against), which is the honest use of a public figure.

### What this does to NR-012's restored table

It is retired **as it stands** and replaced by this item's profile view — the right question, now
with content it is entitled to show. Concretely: rival rows lose their exact balances and gain
four banded axes; the player's own row keeps exact figures. Its home moves off nav slot 8
(Diplomacy), as the item already requires.

### Determinism

Unchanged and load-bearing. Banding is a deterministic bucketing of a fixed-point quantity with
explicit boundaries (a value exactly on a boundary must land in a defined band — do not leave it
to float comparison), ranks have an explicit tie-break, and any walk over corporations is a
sorted walk. Same rule as BL-222's first-industrialiser argmax.

### Still genuinely open after this

- **The band boundaries and axis normalisation** — real tuning, wants the live economy, not a
  paragraph. Promote with placeholder bands and tune against a running campaign.
- **Where the profile lives on screen.** BL-266 has just settled that the Selection band rests on
  the player's own corporation, which is the natural host for the player's OWN standing; the
  comparison view across all corporations is a ledger. That split looks right but is a layout
  call and is Ben's.

## RATIFIED 2026-08-03 (Ben, NR-022)

Ben ratified the six-call package **as written** — no substitutions. The diegetic publication
route is confirmed (not the cheaper meta route), the four-axis profile stands with **no total
ever**, and rival figures stay **banded** rather than exact. The banding is the load-bearing
piece: it is what lets a comparison surface show every corporation at once without violating
BL-068's competitor-visibility rule, which the restored NR-012 table could not do.

The item is promote-ready as designed; nothing further is owed from Ben on it.
items.resolution: FIRST SLICE LANDED 2026-08-06 (docs/development/req/requirements.json § corp-standing-profile): src/world/standing.{hpp,cpp} computes reach/capital/market-share, banded for rivals (never a number), exact for the player, no total row ever — src/ui/corporation_panel.cpp's old raw-balance table retired. standing_harness 41/41 PASS. Kept a SEPARATE quantity from corp_ai's utility scorer per Call 5.
